sections.t: Precursor B Cell Neoplasms B-lymphoblastic leukemias/lymphomas
sections.html:
Original page 7

•Definition: They are neoplasms of hematopoietic progenitors committed to B lineage differentiation.

•Subtypes:

–B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with high hyperdiploidy

–B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with high hypodiploidy

–B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with iAMP21

–B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with BCR::ABL1 fusion

–B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with BCR::ABL1 like features

–B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with KMT2A rearrangement

–B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with ETV6::RUNX1 fusion

–B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with ETV6::RUNX1-like features

–B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with TCF3::PBX1 fusion

–B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with IGH::IL3 fusion

–B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with TCF3::HLF fusion

–B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with other defined genetic alterations

–B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, NOS N.B.: In the absence of complete testing for genetic abnormalities, definitive subclassification may not be possible and the category B-ALL/LBL, NFC (not further classified) should be used.

•Epidemiology: 75% of all cases aged < 6 years with a second smaller peak in the 5th decade. It is the most common leukemia in the pediatric age group.

•Etiology

–Unknown.

–Association with Down syndrome and other constitutional genetic disorders. 7

Original page 8

–Association with single nucleotide polymorphisms in GATA3, ARID5B, IKZF1, CEBPE, CDNK2A and CDNK2B genes. However, true familial B-ALL is rare, and is sometimes associated with mutations in PAX5, ETV6, and TP53.

•Pathogenesis:

–The postulated normal counterpart is a hematopoietic precursor cell committed to B lineage.

–Multiple molecular pathways seem to be affected for leukemogenesis.

•Clinical picture:

–Symptoms of bone marrow failure

–Lymphadenopathy

–Hepatosplenomegaly

–Bone pain and arthralgias

–Common head and neck presentations especially in children.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–CBC: thrombocytopenia, anemia and/or neutropenia. The leukocyte count is often elevated, but may be normal or decreased.

–Bone marrow aspiration: Lymphoblasts vary from small cells with scant cytoplasm, condensed chromatin, and indistinct nucleoli to larger cells with moderate pale blue-gray cytoplasm with occasional vacuolation, dispersed chromatin, and multiple variably prominent nucleoli. Nuclei may be round or show convolutions. Coarse, cytoplasmic azurophilic granules may be seen in roughly 10% of cases, and cytoplasmic pseudopods may be present (hand-mirror cells). N.B.: Hematogones have a similar appearance, but with a higher nuclear-to cytoplasmic ratio, more uniform dispersed chromatin, and no discernible nucleoli. Discrimination requires immunophenotyping.

–Bone marrow biopsy: Blasts form mid-marrow sheets or loose collections that displace or admix with normal marrow elements. The lymphoblasts have a relatively uniform appearance with scant cytoplasm, round to oval to indented or 8

Original page 9

convoluted nuclei, fine chromatin, and variably distinct nucleoli. Mitotic figures vary in number.

–Cytochemistry:

○Negative MPO

○Blasts may stain light grey and weakly with Sudan Black B when granules are present.

○Sodium fluoride sensitive non-specific esterase may show multifocal punctate or Golgi staining

○Periodic acid-Schiff may show coarse chunky cytoplasmic staining.

–Immunophenotyping

○Positive expression (in combination or with an intensity approaching their normal B counterparts) of the B lineage-associated antigens CD19, cCD79a, CD22 (cytoplasmic and surface) and PAX5

○MPO, CD13, CD33 and CD66c may be expressed particularly in cases with t(9;22), but are not indicative of myeloid lineage except if criteria of lineage assignment are fulfilled.

○CD45 expression is lower than mature lymphocytes

○CD10 is often of moderate to high intensity,

○CD20, TdT and CD34 are low to absent

○Immunophenotypic stages: Pro-B (CD19, cCD79, cCD22, TdT), Common-B (CD10), Pre-B (cytoplasmic mu) and Transitional Pre-B (heavy chain without light chains). This staging is of limited clinical utility in contrast to genetic classification.

○Immunophenotypic differences from hematogones are useful for the identification of residual leukemia following therapy. Leukemic blasts show decreased expression of CD45, increased or decreased expression of CD10, 9

Original page 10

increased CD19, decreased expression of CD38 and CD81, increased and uniform CD58, and increased CD66c, CD73, CD86, CD123 and CD304.

–Genetic tests (thefundamental basis for subclassification): See “subtypes”: Familial cases: Germline testing for predisposition should be considered.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis:

–Prognosis is relatively favorable, and more so in children than adults.

–Adverse prognostic factors:

○Age (10 years)

○Elevated white count (>50,000 cells/cmm)

○Slow blast clearance with initial therapy

○Certain genomic entities (e.g. hypodiploidy)

○Presence of residual disease at defined time points early after therapy (End of Induction or Consolidation)

○CNS disease. 10

Original page 11

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of lymphoblasts defined by a karyotype comprising 51-65 chromosomes, characterized by recurrent, non-random gains of one or more copies of entire chromosomes, usually chromosomes X, 4, 6, 10, 14, 17, 18 and 21 in the absence of type-defining translocations.

•Epidemiology: Rare in infants but high hyperdiploidy is most frequent in children and less common in adults.

•Pathogenesis: High hyperdiploidy is the main driver with possible mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)-RAS signaling pathway (FLT3, NRAS, KRAS and PTPN11 genes).

•Genetic tests:

–It is identified by chromosomal analysis, FISH, flowcytometric DNA index or SNP arrays.

–The most frequent affected chromosomes are X, 4, 6, 10, 14, 17, and 18, and trisomy/tetrasomy 21.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis:

–It has a very favorable prognosis.

–Outcome depends on the specific chromosomal gains.

–Adverse risk factors: Advanced patient age and high white cell count. 11

Original page 12

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of lymphoblasts of B lineage defined by the presence of less than or equal to 43 chromosomes. N.B.: Near-diploid cases (44-45 chromosomes) are not included in this category because they do not share its poor prognosis.

•Subtypes:

–Near-haploid (24-31 chromosomes)

–Low-hypodiploid (32-39 chromosomes)

–High-hypodiploid (40-43 chromosomes)

•Epidemiology: Rare in children and the frequency increases with age.

•Etiology: 50% of pediatric low-hypodiploid cases have a germline TP53 mutation (LiFraumeni syndrome).

•Pathogenesis: Loss of P53, the most prominent tumor suppressor.

•Genetic tests: Karyotype, Flowcytometry DNA Index, FISH, and SNP arrays are all useful in establishing the diagnosis.

–Near-haploidy: Alterations in receptor tyrosine kinase and RAS pathway signaling, IKZF3 deletions, and focal deletions of a histone gene cluster at 6p22.

–Low-hypodiploidy: TP53 alterations somatic or germline, associated with Li- Fraumeni syndrome, IKZF2 deletions and RB1 mutations

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Differential diagnosis: Masked near-haploid and low-hypodiploidy: Cases may undergo doubling, resulting in a “pseudohyperdiploid” or near-triploid clone containing up to 78 chromosomes: The two subtypes may be differentiated by: 12

Original page 13

○SNP array analysis, demonstrating copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity for doubled monosomic chromosomes.

○The DNA index assessed by flowcytometry if distinct peaks representing the hypodiploid and doubled clones are both detectable.

○FISH and karyotype demonstrating characteristic patterns of chromosome gain and loss.

•Prognosis: Poor prognosis. 13

Original page 14

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of B-lineage lymphoblasts, defined by the presence of gains and gross rearrangements involving the long arm of chromosome 21.

•Epidemiology: Usually older children and is rare in adults.

•Etiology:

–Constitutional Robertsonian translocation between chromosomes 15 and 21, rob(15;21)(q10;q10)c

–Carriers of constitutional ring chromosomes 21, r(21)c.

•Pathogenesis: Breakage-fusion-bridge cycles, chromosomal missegregation and chromothripsis.

•Genetic tests:

–Karyotyping supported by FISH using a probe for the RUNX1 gene, which detects additional copies of the RUNX1 signal. FISH definition is ≥5 copies of RUNX1 per cell, with ≥3 or more copies on a single abnormal chromosome 21.

–SNP array profile of chromosome 21.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Treatment with more intensive therapy overcomes this adverse risk. 14

Original page 15

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of lymphoblasts of B lineage defined by the presence of rearrangement between the BCR gene on chromosome 22q.11.2 and the ABL1 oncogene on chromosome 9q34.1.

•Epidemiology: The proportion increases with age.

•Pathogenesis: The chimeric BCR::ABL1 protein has a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. The majority of cases have the 190kDa fusion protein with few cases have the 210kDa fusion protein.

•Flowcytometry: Positive B-lineage markers with expression of CD13, CD33 and CD25.

•Genetic tests: Karyotyping, FISH, PCR, DNA or RNA sequencing.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis:

–Incorporation of tyrosine kinase inhibitors has significantly improved the long-term survival rates.

–MRD is a strong predictor of disease relapse and overall survival.

–IKZF1 alterations are associated with poor response to TKIs and worse overall survival. 15

sections.t: B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with BCR::ABL1 like features
sections.html:
Original page 16

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of B lymphoblasts with DNA alterations that induce a phenotype similar to that of BCR::ABL1+ B-ALL, without the pathognomonic BCR::ABL1 rearrangement.

•Epidemiology: The incidence is higher in adolescents and young adults and in Down Syndrome. The male-to-female ratio is ~2:1.

•Pathogenesis:

–Mutations or rearrangements that constitutively activate JAK/STAT, ABL-class, or other kinase signaling pathways as rearrangements of CRLF2 (cytokine receptor- like factor 2) with IGH (t(X/Y;14)) or P2RY8 (intra-chromosomal deletion in the pseudo-autosomal region of chr.X/Y) that lead to aberrant expression of CRLF2.

–There may be additional mutations (CRLF2 p.F232C), activating mutations of JAK1 (most commonly p.V658F), JAK2 (most commonly codon R683) or IL7RA lead to constitutive JAK/STAT activation downstream of CRLF2.

–There may be JAK2 gene fusions or EPOR rearrangements

–There may be alterations in SH2B3, IL2RB, and TYK2 genes and also activate JAK/STAT.

•Immunophenotyping:TSLPR (encoded by CRLF2) overexpression by flowcytometry (CRLF2 rearrangement).

•Genetic tests:

–Whole transcriptome analysis.

–Quantitative real-time PCR of selected gene sets may be a valid alternative. Multiplex reverse-transcriptase PCR can be used to rapidly detect the most common gene fusions

–The majority of cases are cytogenetically cryptic.

–Break-apart FISH probes are available to identify the major rearrangements (involving ABL1, ABL2, CRLF2, JAK2 and PDGFRB as 3' partners). 16

Original page 17

–DNA and RNA sequencing can provide additional information on JAK/STAT and RAS pathway mutations and detect more rare rearrangements (e.g. ETV6::NTRK3, FLT3 rearrangements).

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: It is associated with high-risk features, as elevated leukocyte count at diagnosis and poor treatment response. Absence of IKZF1 alterations may have better prognosis. 17

sections.t: B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with KMT2A rearrangement
sections.html:
Original page 18

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of lymphoblasts of B lineage defined by the presence of a rearrangement between KMT2A and any of a large number of fusion partners.

•Epidemiology: 70-80% of leukemia in infants and is less common in older children and then becomes increasingly common with age into adulthood.

•Etiology: The etiology is unknown. In infants and young children, rearrangement is acquired in utero.

•Pathogenesis: KMT2A is a histone H3 lysine 4 methylase. Rearrangements typically delete the methyltransferase domain and fuse KMT2A to a gene involved in transcription elongation. This results in upregulation of HOXA genes. There may be additional alterations of epigenetic modifiers or MAP kinase genes, including FLT3.

•Immunophenotyping: CD19+, CD10-, CD24- and are often positive for the myeloid markers CD15 and CD65s as well as the neural/glial antigen NG2. TdT negativity is also relatively frequent.

•Genetic tests:

–The seven most common fusion partners are AFF1, MLLT3, MLLT1, MLLT10, AFDN, EPS15 and AFF3.

–Rearrangements can be “cryptic” by karyotype and/or FISH.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: It has a poor prognosis. 18

sections.t: B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with ETV6::RUNX1 fusion
sections.html:
Original page 19

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of B lineage lymphoblasts defined by the presence of rearrangement between the ETV6 gene on chromosome 12p13.2 and the RUNX1 gene on chromosome 21q22.1

•Epidemiology: It is the most common in childhood B-ALL/LBL (2 - 10 years). It is extremely rare in adults and infants.

•Etiology: The ETV6::RUNX1 is an early event necessary but not sufficient for leukemogenesis. A specific environmental or immunologic trigger is unknown.

•Pathogenesis:

–Cell of origin: B-cell progenitor.

–The ETV6::RUNX1 fusion protein interferes with normal function of the transcription factor RUNX1 and other proteins.

•Immunophenotyping:

–Relatively specific phenotype: Negative or partially positive CD9, CD20 and CD66c.

–Positive CD27 and low-to-negative CD44.

–Frequent expression of .Myeloid markers, especially CD13 and CD33

•Genetic tests: The ETV6::RUNX1 translocation is identifiable by FISH, RT-PCR, and RNA sequencing (not by cytogenetics)..

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Very favorable prognosis. 19

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with ETV6::RUNX1-like features

Original page 20

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of lymphoblasts of B-cell lineage characterized by a gene expression profile similar to B-ALL with ETV6::RUNX1 in absence of the ETV6::RUNX1 translocation.

•Epidemiology: It is more frequent in childhood and uncommon in adults.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: Combined ETV6 and IKZF1 rearrangements or deletions lead to RUNX1 disruption. ETV6 partners include BCL2L14, BORCS5, CREBBP, MSH6, NID1 and PMEL.

•Immunophenotyping: Positive CD27 and low-to-negative CD44.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Still undefined. 20

sections.t: B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with TCF3::PBX1 fusion
sections.html:
Original page 21

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of lymphoblasts of B lineage defined by the presence of rearrangement between the TCF3 gene on chromosome 19 and the PBX1 gene on chromosome 1. Cases with TCF3 partners other than PBX1 are not included.

•Epidemiology: It is relatively common in children and rare in adults.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: The TCF3::PBX1 translocation fusion protein is an early lesion necessary but not sufficient for leukemogenesis as it is a transcriptional activator that also interferes with the normal function of the transcription factors encoded by TCF3 and PBX1.

•Immunophenotyping:

–Strong positive CD9, dim to negative CD34 expression, and at least partial absence of CD20, in addition to CD19 and CD10 expression.

–Cytoplasmic μ heavy chain is frequently positive but not specific for this entity.

•Genetic tests: The TCF3::PBX1 (chromosome 19) is detectable by karyotype, FISH and molecular methods. There may be loss of the derivative chromosome 1.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: With modern intensive therapy, it is associated with intermediate to relatively favorable clinical outcomes. 21

sections.t: B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with IGH::IL3 fusion
sections.html:
Original page 22

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of lymphoblasts of B lineage defined by the juxtaposition of the IGH enhancer and the IL3 promoter with characteristic peripheral blood and bone marrow eosinophilia.

•Epidemiology: This is a very rare type mostly reported in children and young adults with a male predominance.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: Balanced t(5;14)(q31.1;q32) that joins the IGH enhancer (14q32) to the IL3 gene promoter (5q31.1) resulting in IL3 overexpression that drives the leukemic clone and induces eosinophil maturation in the bone marrow with reactive eosinophilia.

•Clinical picture: Asymptomatic eosinophilia or clinical manifestations of hypereosinophilic syndrome with organomegaly, dyspnoea, skin involvement, neurological symptoms, thrombo-embolic events, and eosinophilic cardiomyopathy.

•Peripheral blood and bone marrow: Increased eosinophils and variable numbers of lymphoblastswith normal or slightly decreased hemoglobin and platelets.

•Immunophenotyping: Positive CD19 and CD10with possible expression of myeloid markers, CD33 and/or CD13. Both lymphoblasts and eosinophils express the IL3 receptor, CD123.

•Genetic tests: The t(5;14)(q31.1;q32) can be detected by karyotype or FISH.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: There are too few cases to be certain about prognosis but generally it has an intermediate prognosis with poor response to treatment. 22

sections.t: B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with TCF3::HLF fusion
sections.html:
Original page 23

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of B lymphoblasts defined by the presence of rearrangement between TCF3 at 19p13.3 and HLF at 17q22.

•Epidemiology: It is rare mostly reported in children and is very rare in adults.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: The TCF3::HLF fusion consists of the transactivation domains of TCF3 fused to the DNA-binding and dimerization domains of HLF. Its expression leads to transcriptional reprogramming toward an immature state.

•Clinical picture: Hypercalcemia (Parathyroid hormone-related peptide), renal impairment and coagulopathy.

•Immunophenotyping: CD19 expression is typically high, but this is not specific.

•Genetic tests: Karyotype, FISH, and molecular methods are useful in establishing the diagnosis.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Incurable despite treatment intensification and allogeneic stem cell transplantation. 23

Original page 24

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with other defined genetic alterations

•Definition: It is an unregulated clonal proliferation of B lymphoblasts that have specific defining genetic abnormalities of the provisional subtypes.

•Epidemiology: 10-15% of pediatric B-ALL and 20-35% of adult B-ALL

•Etiology: The initiating causes are unknown although genetic risk factors predispose for some cases as the germline variants in hematopoietic transcription factor, PAX5.

•Subtypes and Pathogenesis:

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, NOS

Original page 27

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of lymphoblasts of B lineage that include B-ALL/LBL lacking genetic abnormalities defining other B-ALL/LBL types.

•Epidemiology: 5-10% of B-ALL/LBL

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: Cumulative dysregulations of key regulatory pathways of self-renewal, cell proliferation, apoptosis, differentiation, and/or their signaling pathways.

•Genetic tests: Other definitive and provisional subtypes must be excluded.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Intermediate prognosis in children. 27

Mature B cell Neoplasms

Original page 28

28

Original page 29

•Definition: They are clonal malignancies characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of mature B lymphoid cells.

•Epidemiology:

–They accountfor more than 80% of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

–The median age at diagnosis is 66 years for NHL.

–They are more in men.

–They are more in Caucasians.

•Origin: The origin of cells in mature B-cell neoplasms ranges in differentiation from naïve B cells resting lymphoid cells that have surface immunoglobulin but have not yet encountered antigens to mature plasma cells, which produce immunoglobulins in response to previous antigen exposure.

29

Original page 30

•Clinical presentation: The clinical presentation varies greatly depending on the type of lymphoma and the areas of involvement:

–Some are indolent with insidious onset presenting only by slow growing lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or cytopenias with waxing and waning lymphadenopathy for years. Examples include follicular lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma, and splenic marginal zone lymphoma.

–Others are highly aggressive presenting acutely or subacutely with a rapidly growing mass and systemic B symptoms as fever, night sweats and weight loss and result in death within weeks if left untreated. Examples include diffuse large B cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma. 30

Original page 31

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Complete blood count.

–Examination of peripheral blood or tissue biopsy.

–Immunophenotyping.

–Genetic tests.

–Clonality can be detected by light chain restriction or clonal immunoglobulin genes rearrangement.

–Renal and hepatic function and srum albumin, calcium and uric acid.

–Serum lactate dehydrogenase.

–Serum beta 2 microglobulin.

–Lumbar puncture is required if there is clinical suspicion of CNS involvement.

•2022 WHO classification of mature B cell neoplasms:

✓Splenic B-cell lymphomas and leukemias

✓Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma

✓Marginal zone lymphoma

✓Follicular lymphoma

✓Mantle cell lymphoma

✓Transformations of indolent B-cell lymphomas

✓Large B cell lymphoma

✓Burkitt lymphomas

✓KSHV/HHV8-associated B-cell lymphoid proliferations and lymphomas

✓Lymphoid proliferations and lymphomas associated with immune deficiency and dysregulation

✓Hodgkin lymphoma

✓Plasma cell neoplasms and other diseases with paraproteins 31

Original page 32

Pre-neoplastic and neoplastic small lymphocytic proliferations

•They include:

–Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma

–Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis 32

Original page 33

•Definition: It is an asymptomatic condition characterized by the presence of a monoclonal B-cell population in the absence of lymphadenopathy, organomegaly or any features diagnostic of another B-lymphoproliferative disorder.

•Subtypes:

–Monoclonal B cell lymphocytosis, low count or clonal B-cell expansion Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (CLL/SLL) type: Clonal 9 CLL/SLL-type B-cell count below 0.5 x 10 /L with no other diagnostic features of B-lymphoproliferative disorder.

–Monoclonal B cell lymphocytosis, CLL/SLL type: Monoclonal CLL/SLL-type cell 99 count ≥0.5 x 10 /L and total B-cell count less than 5 x 10 /L with no other diagnostic features of CLL/SLL.

–MBL, non-CLL/SLL type: Any monoclonal non-CLL/SLL type B-cell expansion with no symptoms or diagnostic features of another mature B-cell neoplasm with the majority of cases having features consistent with a marginal zone origin.

•Clinical picture:

–Asymptomatic.

–Fatigue, weight loss and night sweats.

–Immune impairment with suboptimal responses to vaccination and frequent infection.

•Epidemiology: CLL/SLL-type: 5% of people aged 40-50 years, 5-25% of people aged 65 – 80 years; and 50-75% of people over 90 years, with a similar age distribution of CLL/SLL and median age at diagnosis of 70-75 years.

•Etiology: Unknown but genetic predisposition to CLL/SLL-type is evident from family studies, with multiple single-nucleotide polymorphisms.

•Pathogenesis:

–BCR-signaling plays a central role. 33

Original page 34

–Genetic abnormalities prevalent in CLL/SLL can be found in CLL/SLL-type with a lower frequency.

–Genetic abnormalities of post-germinal-center B cell neoplasms, as MYD88 mutations, are common in non-CLL/SLL-type.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Morphology of CLL/SLL-type: Similar to that of CLL/SLL

–Morphology of non-CLL/SLL-type: Centrocyte-like cells.

–Bone marrow and lymph node investigations are not indicated.

–Bone marrow: Cells in CLL/SLL type may form focal aggregates or diffuse lymphocytosis and represent < 30% of bone marrow cells.

–Flowcytometry:

○Light chain kappa: lambda ratio of >3:1 or 25% of mature B-cells lacking sIg.

○CLL/SLL type: Coexpression of CD5 and CD23 and positive CD43, CD200 and ROR1 on >20% of the clonal CD19+ B-cells with weak expression of CD20, CD79b, CD81 and immunoglobulin light chain and negative CD10

○Non-CLL/SLL type: Similar to marginal zone lymphoma or lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (negative CD5 and CD10 with abnormal intensity of B-cell markers or the light chains).

–Genetic tests:

○No diagnostic molecular abnormalities.

○13q14 deletions are common in CLL/SLL-type

○MYD88 mutation is common in non-CLL/SLL-type.

○TP53 mutation/deletion may be detectable in some cases.

•Diagnostic criteria

–Essential criteria:

○Demonstration of a monoclonal B-cell population (light-chain restriction or lack of surface light chain expression by flowcytometry or monoclonal 34

Original page 35

9 immunoglobulin gene rearrangement) with a peripheral B-cell count of < 5 x 10 /L.

○Absence of lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or any features diagnostic of another B lymphoproliferative disorder. 9

➢Low count MBL/Clonal B-cell Expansion: Clonal B-cell count < 0.5 x 10 /L and typical CLL/SLL phenotype 9

➢CLL/SLL-type MBL: Clonal B-cell count ≥0.5 x 10 /L and typical CLL/SLL phenotype

➢Non-CLL/SLLMBL: Any clonal B-cell expansion without the typical CLL/SLL phenotype

–Desirable criterion: Expression patterns that would be atypical for CLL/SLL, e.g., strong CD20 / CD79b / CD81 / sIg, or weak/undetectable CD43 /CD200 / ROR1 expression, may also warrant further investigation to exclude other B- lymphoproliferative disorder.

•Prognosis:

–Progression to CLL/SLL: 0.5-2%/year among individuals with CLL/SLL type. The risk of progression to CLL/SLL is higher if: 9

○Clonal B-cell count is > 3 x 10 /L

○Unmutated IGHV genes

○Serum β2-microglobulin > 3.5 g/L.

–Low-count MBL/clonal B-cell expansion: Negligible risk of developing CLL/SLL in general, but can occur in familial CLL/SLL. 35

sections.t: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)/ Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL)
sections.html:
Original page 36

•Definitions:

▪CLL is a neoplasm composed of monomorphic small mature B cells that co-express 9 CD5 and CD23 with a count of 5 x 10/L, or more in the peripheral blood.

▪SLL is a neoplasm composed of monomorphic small mature B cells that co-express 9 CD5 and CD23 with a circulating CLL cell count less than 5x10/L and documented nodal (e.g., lymphadenopathy >15 mm), splenic, or other extramedullary involvement.

•Normal counterpart: An antigen-experienced mature CD5+B cell with mutated or unmutated IGHVgenes.

•Epidemiology:

–It is the most common leukemia of adults in fair-skinned populations while being rare in Asian countries and in Latin Americans indicating a genetic predisposition.

–It can present in younger adults but the incidence increases with age, especially older than 70 years.

–Male-to-female ratio in Western populations is 1.5-2.1:1.

•Etiology:

–Unknown.

–A theory suggests that it is resulted from stimulation of the B cell by a limited set of antigens promoting division of precursor cells and clonal evolution. This theory is supported by the finding that B-cell receptors of CLL cells show very similar antigen-binding sites, coded by both heavy and light chain genes.

–Genetic susceptibility as evidenced by: 36

Original page 37

○Family members of patients with CLL or related lymphomas, such as lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma and mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), have a 5 to 8-fold increased risk of CLL.

○Over 40 single nucleotide polymorphisms are associated with the risk of CLL.

•Pathogenesis:

–Cell of origin: Antigen-experienced, memory-like B cells differentiated via follicular (positive somatic hypermutation) or extra-follicular (Un-mutated) maturation pathways.

–Microenvironment: Growth occurs in proliferation centers within lymph nodes, where they interact with T-helper cells, mesenchymal stromal cells, and macrophages, leading to B cell receptor signaling which drives cell growth with selection and expansion of cells bearing B cell receptors specific for certain antigens

–The most frequent chromosomal aberrations:

○del(13q): Loss of microRNA which regulates expression of anti-apoptotic and cell cycle regulatory proteins.

○del(11q): Loss of ATM

○del(17p): Loss of TP53.

○Trisomy 12: Involved genes are unknown and more common in SLL than CLL.

–The most frequently mutated genes: NOTCH1, ATM, SF3B1, TP53, and BIRC3.

–Untreated cases rarely acquire new genetic lesions but large clonal shifts can occur following treatment as TP53 aberrations, MYC gain, and CDKN2A loss.

–Epigenetics: Three subtypes according to the DNA methylation signatures:

○Memory-like CLL (m-CLL): DNA methylation signatures is similar to germinal-center experienced B cells.

○Naïve-like CLL (n-CLL): DNA methylation signatures is similar to germinal- center inexperienced B cells 37

Original page 38

○Intermediate DNA methylation profile (i-CLL)

•Clinical features:

–Most cases are asymptomatic.

–Lymphadenopathy. 38

Original page 39

–Splenomegaly.

–Symptoms of cytopenia due to bone marrow infiltration or autoimmune mechanisms as symptoms of anemia, or thrombocytopenia and infection, mostly pulmonary. Infection also may result from hypogammaglobulinemia or defective cellular immunity

–Symptoms of hypermetabolism or B symptoms: Chronic fatigue, night fever, fever of unknown origin and/or night sweating, loss of weight (>10% of body weight over a period of 6 months) and gout.

–Rapid and asymmetric growth of lymph nodes or extranodal masses is suggestive of transformation.

•Complications: 1-Infection. 2-Second malignancy: Melanoma, sarcoma and squamous cell carcinoma. 3-Therapy related acute myeloid leukemia. 4-Pure red cell aplasia 5-Progression and transformation:

▪Progression into high-grade lymphoma:

–Clinical progression is associated with an increase in size and proliferative activity of the malignant cells.

–Proliferation centers may expand with a higher proliferation rate and become confluent. Histologically aggressive CLLs was characterized by proliferation centers broader than a 20x field or becoming confluent.

–The Ki-67 proliferation index becomes more than 40% or mitoses in the proliferation centers more than 2.4. N.B.: These cases have an outcome intermediate between those of typical CLL and classic Richter syndrome.

▪Prolymphocytoid transformation: Increasing prolymphocytes in the blood. 39

Original page 40

N.B: No progression into B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.

▪Progression intodiffuse large B-cell lymphoma (Richter syndrome):

–It occurs in 2-8% of patients.

–It is associated with TP53 and NOTCH1 mutations, CDKN2A deletions, and MYC translocations. N.B.: Most cases of DLBCL type Richter syndrome are clonally related to the previous CLL expressing the same immunoglobulin gene rearrangement, and are IGHV-unmutated with a median survival time of less than 1 year, whereas clonally unrelated cases usually occur in IGHV-mutated CLL with a prognosis identical to that of a de novo DLBCL.

▪Progression intoclassicHodgkin lymphoma: It occurs in than 1% of cases and is characterized by:

–Mostly occur in mutated CLL.

–EBV-positive.

–Unrelated to the CLL clone. N.B.: The diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma in the setting of CLL requires classic Reed- Sternberg cells in an appropriate background. The presence of scattered EBV-positive or sometimes EBV-negative Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of CLL does not fulfil the criteria for the Hodgkin lymphoma. N.B.: EBV-associated lymphoproliferative disorders, including Hodgkin lymphoma may occur in patients with CLL after immunosuppressive therapy.

•Laboratory Diagnosis:

▪Evidence of clonality 1-Light chain restriction: normally κ : λ = 2 : 1. 2-Unique immunoglobulin gene rearrangement. 3-Monoclonal immunophenotyping. 4-Monoclonal genetics. 40

Original page 41

▪Complete blood count:

–Leukocytosis with marked relative and absolute lymphocytosis more than 5 9 X 10/L. There may be neutropenia.

–Red cells are normal in early stages. Anemia may be due to: a-Bone marrow infiltration. b-Autoimmune hemolytic anemia: diseases associated or triggered by therapy. c-Hypersplenism. d-Red cell aplasia. e-Folate or iron deficiency especially in old age. f-Chronic blood loss due to thrombocytopenia.

–Platelets: There may be thrombocytopenia: a-Bone marrow infiltration. b-Autoimmune thrombocytopenia.

▪Blood Film:

–Small lymphocytes with clumped chromatin and scant cytoplasm.

–Smudge or basket cells.

–Prolymphocytes which are larger cells with irregular nuclear contours, more dispersed chromatin and more abundant cytoplasm. They constitute less than 15% of the lymphoid cells. N.B.: Cases with a higher proportion of these cells but less than 55% prolymphocytes have been called atypical CLL. They are characterized by trisomy 12 and strong positivity for surface immunoglobulin, CD20, and FMC7. N.B.: The finding of more than 55% prolymphocytes defines B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia. 41

Original page 42

▪Bone marrow aspirate: Infiltration by small lymphocytes and few prolymphocytes. Lymphocytes are mostly more than 30%.

▪Bone marrow biopsy:

–Pattern of infiltration: Interstitial, nodular, mixed (nodular and interstitial), or diffuse. Diffuse infiltration has a bad prognosis. Para-trabecular infiltration is not typical.

–Proliferation centers can be observed, but not as prominent as in lymph nodes.

–Follicular dendritic cells may be present.

▪Immunophenotyping:

○In typical cases B cells show:

○Light chain restriction.

–Co-expression of CD19 and CD5.

–Strong positive expression CD23.

–Dim expression of surface lgM/lgD, CD20, CD22, and CD79b.

–FMC7 is usually negative or only weakly expressed.

–Negative expression CD10.

–Positive expression of CD43.

–Strong positive expression of CD200.

–Cyclin D1 is negative.

–CD20 is usually and its detection is important for decision of treatment by anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies.

–ZAP70 and CD38 may be positive with a bad prognosis.

○Some cases have an atypical immunophenotype and should be differentiated from other type of B-cell neoplasm, as splenic marginal zone lymphoma. The atypical immunophenotypes include either:

–Negative expression of CD5 or CD23. 42

Original page 43

–Strong positive expression of surface immunoglobulin, FMC7 or CD79b.

✓Typical CLL: 4-5.

✓Atypical CLL: 3.

✓NHL with leukemia: 0-2.

▪Genetic tests:

○Antigen receptor genes:

–IGHV genes are mutated (i.e. less than 98% identity with the germline) in 50- 70% of cases and unmutated with more active BCR signaling (i.e. 98% or more identity) in 30-50%.

–BCR stereotype: 30% of patients have very similar, if not identical, immunoglobulin sequences.

–CLL B-cell receptors recognize both foreign and self-antigens.

–Autonomous signaling: CLL B-cells producing monoclonal immunoglobulins recognizing itself on the same or adjacent cells.

○Genetic abnormalities and oncogenes:

–No specific genetic markers. These findings are prognostic and not diagnostic.

–Cytogenetic abnormalities in 80-90% of cases:

➢Deletions 13q14.3 involving miR-16-1 and miR- 15a in 50% of cases and translocations involving the 13q14 region which are associated with miR- 16-1 and miR-15a deletions in 2% of cases.

➢Trisomy 12 or partial trisomy 12q13 in 20% of cases. 43

Original page 44

➢Gains of 2p in 7% of cases.

➢Loss of 14q in 4% of cases.

➢Gain of 8q24 involving MYC in 3% of cases.

➢t(14;18)(q32;q21) IGH;BCL2 as a secondary change in 2% of cases, usually with mutated IGHV and t(14;19) (q32;q13) IGH;BCL3 in occasional cases with unmutated IGHV genes.

➢Complex rearrangements in 2% of cases, mainly with unmutated IGHV genes in association with TP53 mutations.

➢Other deletions are less common:

✓11q22-23 involving ATM and BIRC3.

✓17p13 involving TP53.

✓6q21.

–Gene mutation in 3- 15% of cases involving TP53, NOTCH1, SF3B1, ATM, BIRC3, POT1, MYD88 and many other genes. Mutation of TP53, BIRC3, NOTCH1, and SF3B1 are more at relapse.

–There are three epigenetic subgroups with different biological characteristics according to the methylation pattern:

➢Naive-like CLL resembling naive B cells and has mainly unmutated IGHV.

➢Memory-like CLL which resembles memory B cells and has mutated IGHV genes.

➢Intermediate CLL which is intermediate between naive and memory like CLL and has mutated IGHV genes with a more aggressive clinical behavior than that of the memory-like subgroup. 44

Original page 45

▪Other laboratory tests:

–A small paraprotein, usually of lgM type in 10% of cases.

–Hypogammaglobulinemia in 30% of cases at diagnosis and increases over time to 60% in advanced disease.

–Biochemical tests: High levels of serum LDH and uric acid.

•Recommended investigations for prognosis:

•Diagnostic criteria: 45

Original page 46

•Differential diagnosis: Causes of lymphocytosis:

➢Reactive lymphocytosis: Lymphocytes are reactive with less condensed chromatin and more cytoplasm and are polyclonal with no light chain restriction and negative for CD5:

–Viral infection.

–Thyrotoxicosis.

–Chronic inflammation.

–Malignancy.

–Autoimmune diseases.

–Post-splenectomy.

➢Neoplastic lymphocytosis: 46

Original page 47

–Acute lymphoblastic leukemia: Blasts are more than 20% in peripheral blood and/or bone marrow.

–Other lymphoproliferative disorders:

○B cell lymphoproliferative disorders:

○T and NK cell lymphoproliferative disorders: CD3(+), CD2(+) and CD5(+). 47

Original page 48

•Staging:

–Rai staging:

Original page 49

•Prognosis:

–Isolated deletion in 13q14 has a favorable prognosis but cases with a high proportion of cells with isolated 13q deletion, however, do not do as well.

–Clinical staging:

○Low risk: Rai 0 and Binet A.

○Intermediate risk: Rai I or II and Binet B.

○High risk: Rai III or IV and Binet C.

–Bad prognostic factors include:

○Peripheral blood:

➢Rapid lymphocyte doubling time in the blood less than 12 months.

➢Presence of >15% prolymphocytes in peripheral blood

➢Elevated serum thymidine kinase.

➢Elevated serum beta-2 microglobulin. 49

Original page 50

➢Elevated lactate dehydrogenase

○Bone marrow:

➢Diffuse infiltration of the bone marrow.

➢Presence of plasma cells in marrow biopsies

○Immunophenotyping:

➢Expression of ZAP70, CD38, or CD49d.

➢Higher expression of CD23 in the proliferating center.

➢High levels of soluble CD23.

○Genetics:

➢Unmutated IGHV genes.

➢Subset #2: It is a stereotyped B cell receptor utilizing the IGHV3-21 gene.

➢Deletion 11q.

➢Deletion 17p.

➢Complex karyotype.

➢TP53 abnormalities as deletion 17p13 and TP53 mutations don’t respond to fludarabine-containing treatments.

➢Mutations in ATM, NOTCH1, SF3B1, and BIRC3.

○Epigenetics: Naive- like cases is worse than the intermediate subgroup and the intermediate group is worse than the memory-like subgroup.

○Response to treatment: Bad response to treatment which is the most important. 50

Splenic B-cell lymphomas and leukemias

Original page 51

1-Hairy cell leukemia 2-Splenic marginal zone lymphoma 3-Splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma 4-Splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukemia with prominent nucleoli “previous called hairy-cell leukemia variant“

▪When it is not possible to establish a definitive classification, when no splenectomy specimen is available, the term “splenic B cell leukemia/lymphoma NOS” is appropriate. 51

Original page 52

•Definition: It is an indolent neoplasm of mature B lymphoid cells with abundant cytoplasm and hairy projections involving peripheral blood, bone marrow and splenic red pulp and bear the BRAF p.V600E somatic mutation in ≥95% of cases.

•Epidemiology:

–It is rare accounting for 2% of all leukemias.

–It occurs mainly in the middle aged to elderly adults with a median age of 60 years, rare in the 20s, and uncommon in children.

–The male to female ratio is 4:1

–The incidence is higher in White versus Black populations.

•Etiology:

▪Precise etiology is unknown.

▪Inherited susceptibility as evidenced by the over-representation of the HLA-DRB11 allele.

▪Farming, exposure to pesticides and exposure to benzene may be risk factors.

•Pathogenesis:

▪Cell of origin: The transcriptional signature is similar to post-germinal center memory B cells, but the corresponding normal cell counterpart is uncertain.

▪Increased proliferation: It is caused by BRAF V600E mutation leading to constitutive activation of mitogen activated protein (MAPK) pathway.

▪Prolonged survival: It is caused by the high BCL2 expression.

▪Filamentous membrane projections: It is caused by the polymerized actin (F-actin) in the cortical cytoskeleton. N.B.: F-actin in normal B cells, is mostly located in the central part of the cell. 52

Original page 53

▪Homing to bone marrow, splenic red bulb and hepatic sinusoids and not to lymph nodes: It is caused by:

–The interaction between the α4β1 integrin on the hairy cells and vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM1) in bone marrow, hepatic and splenic sinusoids.

–Low expression of CCR7 and CXCR5 which control lymph node migration.

–Overexpression of matrix metalloproteinase inhibitors which inhibit the matrix metalloproteinase that degrades the matrix around tumor cells, enabling them to cross tissue boundaries and promote angiogenesis.

–Annexin-A1 blocks the trans-endothelial migration of leukocytes and desensitizes them to chemo-attractants that are produced during inflammatory responses.

▪Pancytopenia: It is caused by:

–The inhibitory cytokines secreted by hairy cells.

–Splenomegaly.

–Bone marrow fibrosis.

▪Reticulin fibrosis: It is caused by the increased fibroblast growth factor and transforming growth factor β.

▪Increased phagocytosis: It is caused by high expression of annexin A1.

•Clinical picture:

–It involvesmainly the bone marrow with few circulating cells.

–Splenomegaly with a left upper quadrant pain

–There may be hepatomegaly.

–It rarely involves lymph nodes, liver, bone, skin, breast or brain.

–Symptoms of bone marrow failure: Weakness and recurrent opportunistic infections. 53

Original page 54

–Less common findings: Vasculitis, bleeding disorders, neurological disorders, skeletal involvement and immune dysfunction.

•Laboratory findings:

▪Complete blood count:

–Pancytopenia.

–Monocytopenia is characteristic.

▪Morphology of hairy cells:

–Size: small to medium-sized.

–Nuclei: Oval or indented kidney-shaped.

–Chromatin: Homogeneous, spongy, ground-glass less clumped than that of a normal lymphocyte.

–Nucleoli: Absent or inconspicuous.

–Cytoplasm: Abundant and pale blue, with circumferential hairy projections. Occasionally, the cytoplasm contains discrete vacuoles or rod-shaped inclusions that represent the ribosome lamellar complexes that have been identified by electron microscopy.

–Electron microscopy:cytoplasmic villi. 54

Original page 55

▪Peripheral blood: Few circulating neoplastic cells.

▪Bone marrow aspiration: Dry tap due to the bone marrow fibrosis.

▪Bone marrow biopsy:

–The abundant cytoplasm and prominent cell borders may produce a fried-egg appearance.

–The primary pattern of infiltration is interstitial or patchy with some preservation of fat and hematopoietic elements. Infiltration may be diffuse in advanced stages giving the honey comb appearance. 55

Original page 56

–Reticulin fibrosis

–Mitotic figures are nearly absent.

▪Cytochemistry: It is strongly positive for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) with granular cytoplasmic positivity. Weak staining is of no diagnostic utility.

▪Immunophenotyping:

–Positive expression of CD19, CD20 and CD24.

–Light Chain restriction.

–Strong expression of surface Ig, FMC7, CD79b and CD22(+).

–Coexpression of CD20, CD22, and CD11c.

–Positive expression of CD103, CD25, CD123, TBX21 (TBET), DBA44, CD200, and cyclin D1 (usually weak).

–CD5 is positive only in 0-2% of cases

–CD10 is positive only in 10-20% of cases.

–V600E-mutant BRAF protein is positive by immunohistochemistry.

–Annexin A1 is the most specific marker being not expressed in any other B-cell lymphoma but it must found to be coexpressed with B-cell antigens as CD20 because it is also expressed by myeloid and some of T cells. So, it is not a suitable marker for monitoring residual disease.

–Monitoring of minimal residual disease:

○Targeting the distinctive HCL profile. 56

Original page 57

○Immunostaining for TBX21.

○Immunostaining for V600E-mutant BRAF protein.

▪Genetic profile:

–Antigen receptor genes

○Somatic hypermutation of IGHV genes in more than 85% of cases indicating a post-germinal center stage of maturation.

○Coexpression of multiple clonally related immunoglobulin isotypes, suggesting arrest at some point during isotype switching.

–Cytogenetic abnormalities and oncogenes:

○No specific cytogenetic abnormality.

○Numerical abnormalities of chromosomes 5 and 7 are rare.

○Translocations are distinctly uncommon.

○BRAF V600E mutation in almost all cases.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Differential Diagnosis::

➢Reactive lymphocytes: Lymphocytes are reactive with less condensed chromatin and more cytoplasm and are polyclonal with no light chain restriction:

–Viral infection. 57

Original page 58

–Thyrotoxicosis.

–Chronic inflammation.

–Malignancy.

–Autoimmune diseases.

–Post-splenectomy.

➢Neoplastic lymphocytes:

–Acute lymphoblastic leukemia: Blasts are more than 20% in peripheral blood and/or bone marrow.

–Other lymphoproliferative disorders:

○B cell lymphoproliferative disorders: Other small B-cell lymphomas with splenomegaly but little or no lymphadenopathy and presence of circulating lymphoid cells with or without villous projections, including splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukemia with prominent nucleoli, splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma, and splenic marginal zone lymphoma:

58

Original page 59

○T and NK cell lymphoproliferative disorders: CD3(+), CD2(+) and CD5(+). 59

Original page 60

➢In some cases, the bone marrow is hypocellular, with a loss of hematopoietic elements, in particular of the granulocytic lineage, which can lead to an incorrect diagnosis of aplastic anemia to be differentiated by immunohistochemistry.

➢Myelodysplastic syndromes and megaloblastic or aplastic anemia: Cases may show some dyserythropoiesis in the form of hyperplastic pro-erythroblasts and basophilic erythroblasts.

•Prognosis and predictive factors:

–It is uniquely sensitive to either interferon α or nucleosides (purine analogues) such as pentostatin and cladribine.

–In refractory or relapsed cases, therapeutic options include chemotherapy combined with rituximab, anti-CD22 immunotoxin therapy, and, more recently, BRAF inhibitors

–Persistence of minimal residual disease after response to treatment correlates with a shorter time to relapse. 60

Original page 61

•Definition: It is an indolent mature B-cell neoplasm primarily presenting in the spleen, preferentially white pulp, often with villous lymphocytes in peripheral blood, with or without involvement of splenic hilar lymph nodes.

•Epidemiology:

–Age: middle-aged and older adults, with a median age in the 7th decade.

–Incidence is slightly higher among males and non-Hispanic whites.

•Etiology:

–Unknown in most cases.

–It may be associated with history of autoimmune conditions or family history of lymphoma.

–Hepatitis C virus may have a role especially when complicated by cryoglobulinemia..

•Pathogenesis:

–Immunoglobulin heavy and light chain genes are clonally rearranged with somatic mutations.

–Hemizygous deletion of 7q31-32.

–Cooccurrence of trisomies of chromosomes 3 and 18.

–Rare: Rearrangement of CDK6 oncogene with immunoglobulin gene loci

–Gene mutations:

○NNK- Splenic marginal zone lymphomas: Mutations affecting NF-κB, including non-canonical pathway genes, NOTCH and KLF2.

○DMT- Splenic marginal zone lymphoma: Mutations in DNA damage response genes, MAPK and TLR signaling genes.

•Clinical picture:

–Splenomegaly or massive splenomegaly

–Symptoms related to cytopenias. 61

Original page 62

–Systemic symptoms, e.g., fever and night sweats, are rare and suggest transformation to an aggressive lymphoma.

–Autoimmune manifestations (acquired angioedema due to C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency, cold agglutinin disease, warm antibody autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and mixed cryoglobulinemia) in 20% of patients

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Peripheral blood:

○Mild-to-moderate lymphocytosis.

○Neoplastic cells are mature small-to-medium-sized lymphoid cells with round nuclei, condensed chromatin and basophilic cytoplasm with short villi, unevenly distributed or concentrated at one or two poles of the cell.

○Morphological heterogeneity with small lymphoid cells, lymphoplasmacytoid cells, lymphocytes with nuclear clefts and/or medium-sized lymphoid cells with relatively abundant pale cytoplasm.

–A low-level paraprotein without significant hyperviscosity in 30% of patients.

–Bone marrow:

○Variable involvement with intertrabecular nodules and interstitial and focally intrasinusoidal infiltration. Diffuse infiltration may occur. Rare cases show marginal zone expansion surrounding reactive follicles.

○CD20 immunostaining is often helpful

○Normal hematopoiesis may be increased, particularly in cases with hypersplenism.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Positive expression of CD20, CD79a, PAX5, FMC7, CD27, CD38 (dim), BCL2, IgM and IgD and negative expression of BCL6, annexin A1, CD103, cyclin D1, SOX11 and LEF1.

○Some cases expresses CD11c, CD123, CD5 (usually weak) CD25, DBA44 or CD43.

○Rare cases are CD10+. 62

Original page 63

–Genetic tests:

○Immunoglobulin heavy and light chain genes are clonally rearranged.

○Deletion 7q31-32 is the sole specific molecular biomarker.

○NOTCH2 and KLF2 mutations.

•Differential diagnosis:

–Other small B-cell lymphomas, such as follicular lymphoma, CLL/SLL, hairy cell leukemia, and mantle cell lymphoma, should be excluded using immunophenotypic and genetic studies.

–Other splenic lymphomas, including hairy cell leukemia, splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukemia with prominent nucleoli: See the table in the differential diagnosis of HCL.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis:

–It is generally indolent, with a median survival exceeding 10 years.

–Transformation into an aggressive lymphoma, low hemoglobin, low platelet count, high lactate dehydrogenase level and occurrence of extra-hilar lymphadenopathy, NOTCH2 mutations, KLF2 mutations and the NNK molecular genotype are poor prognostic biomarker. 63

sections.t: Splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma (SDRPL)
sections.html:
Original page 64

•Definition: It is a small B-cell lymphoma involving the spleen, bone marrow, and peripheral blood, characterized by diffuse infiltration of the splenic red pulp by a monomorphic lymphoid population associated with circulating tumor cells bearing cytoplasmic projections.

•Epidemiology: It is rare with patients are male with a median age under 75 years.

•Etiology: Unknown.

•Pathogenesis:

–Antigen drive evidenced by positive expression of B cell receptor immunoglobulin with somatically hypermutated IGHV genes.

–Mutations and copy number variations in the NOTCH1, NOTCH2, MYD88, TP53, MAP2K1, CCND3, BCOR, ARIDIA-A1, and SYK genes.

•Clinical picture: Pronounced splenomegaly with infrequent B symptoms.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Lymphocytosis

–Neoplastic cells are small to medium-sized cells with round or oval nuclei and clumped chromatin. The cytoplasm is variable in amount and moderately basophilic. Cytoplasmic or villous projections are well-visible, broad-based, and unevenly distributed around the cells with a polar distribution (1 to 4 poles). The nucleolus is small or not visible in the large majority of the cells and is rarely prominent.

–Pancytopenia is infrequent, mostly seen in cases with hypersplenism.

–Serum M component of IgM, IgG, or IgM+G type, has been reported,

–Bone marrow:

○Variable cellularity with sufficient residual hematopoiesis and mild fibrosis.

○Patterns of infiltration: Mainly intrasinusoidal and/or interstitial.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Positive for B cell markers (CD20, CD19, CD79a), and DBA44, and IgG 64

Original page 65

○Negative for CD5, CD23, CD43, cyclin D1, CD21, CD10, CD25, CD38 and Annexin A1.

○Cyclin D3 is expressed in 70% of cases.

○The proliferation index (Ki67) is usually low.

○CD180 is a very useful marker especially if associated with CD200 expression (CD200 median fluorescence /CD180 median fluorescence ratio < 0.5 favors the diagnosis).

–Genetic tests: No molecular test is pathognomonic.

○BRAF p.V600E (NP_004324.2) mutation and mutations in NOTCH2 and KLF2 are not present.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Differential diagnosis: Other splenic small B-cell lymphomas:

○Lymphocytosis is moderate in contrast to splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukemia with hairy cell features.

○Monocytopenia typically seen in hairy cell leukemia is not characteristic of splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma.

○Macroscopic pattern of involvement of the spleen and the pattern of bone marrow infiltration may be helpful.

○Immunophenotypically, CD25, cyclin D1 and Annexin A1, typically expressed in hairy cell leukemia, are absent in splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma.

○The CD200MFI/CD180MFI ratio by FCM can help in the differential diagnosis. 65

sections.t: Splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukemia with prominent nucleoli
sections.html:
Original page 66

•Definition: It is a splenic B-cell neoplasm with some but not all cytomorphologic and immunophenotypic features cells of hairy cell leukemia lacking BRAF mutation and resistant to conventional hairy cell leukemia therapy. Characteristically, the cells have a single large nucleolus.

•Clinical picture:

–Splenomegaly.

–Hepatomegaly may be present.

–Peripheral lymphadenopathy is uncommon.

–Autoimmune phenomena are rare.

•Epidemiology: It is rare with the median age is 71 and a slight male predominance (1.6:1)

•Etiology: Not known.

•Pathogenesis:

–No specific cytogenetic changes have been identified.

–Most cases carry a relatively low load of somatic hypermutation within the clonotypic rearranged IGHV genes.

–Complex karyotypes involving 14q32 as well as 8q24, deletion 17p, and trisomy 12

–BRAF p.V600E (NP_004324.2) mutation is absent.

–MAP2K1 mutations, KMT2C/MLL3 mutations, TP53 mutations and/or 17p deletions, U2AF1 and CCND3 mutations and 7q deletions may be present

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Peripheral blood:

○High lymphocytosis, and cytopenia without monocytopenia.

○Neoplastic cells are medium to large in size with abundant basophilic or pale cytoplasm with fine or poorly defined projections. They typically have a large prominent single nucleolus. The cells are smaller than those of HCL, but occasionally large cells with a bilobed nucleus can be identified. In contrast to HCL, the cells do not have circumferential villous processes. 66

Original page 67

–Bone marrow:

○Normal or increased cellularity, with a variable, often mild, degree of lymphoid infiltration and mild fibrosis.

○Pattern of infiltration: Interstitial and intrasinusoidal. It may be mixed nodular and interstitial or diffuse in later stages of the disease.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Monotypic surface immunoglobulin (more frequently IgG, either alone or with another isotype)

○Positive expression of pan-B cell antigens (CD19, CD20 and CD22, DBA-44), CD11c, CD103 and FMC7

○Negative expression of CD25, Annexin A1, TRAP and CD123.

–Genetic tests: No molecular test is pathognomonic.

•Differential diagnosis: Other splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukemias:

○Cytological atypia and by the presence of a prominent nucleolus.

○Immunophenotyping

○Pattern of infiltration

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis:

–Variable, with half of the patients dying from unrelated causes.

–More aggressive than classical HCL.

–No response to IFN-alpha

–Some patients partially respond to the purine analogues 2’-deoxycoformycin (pentostatin) and 2’-classic Hodgkin lymphoma orodeoxyadenosine (cladribine). 67

Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma

Original page 68

68

Original page 69

•Definition: It is a neoplasm comprising small B lymphocytes, plasmacytoid lymphocytes and plasma cells, usually involving the bone marrow and sometimes lymph nodes and spleen.

•Waldenström Macroglobulinemia: It is the combination of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma in the bone marrow with an IgM monoclonal component in the blood.

•Subtypes:

–IgM Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma/Waldenstrom Macroglobulinemia type.

–Non-IgM Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma /Waldenstrom Macroglobulinemia type: Cases with IgG or IgA monoclonal proteins and those with non-secretory Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma and cases with IgM without bone marrow involvement.

•Epidemiology:

–2% of all hematological malignancies.

–Most patients are of > 65 years or older,

–More common in males and in the white population.

•Etiology:

–Unknown.

–Acquired risk factors: IgM monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and hepatitis C virus infection.

–Familial predisposition in 20% of cases.

•Epidemiology:

–It is the commonest childhood cancer in many countries in equatorial Africa and in Papua New Guinea, where it is considered endemic. Elsewhere, it is less common in children and is considered sporadic.

–It is not possible to identify sporadic cases occurring in endemic areas and vice versa, whereas cases with immune deficiency/dysregulation settings is more readily recognized.

–Geographical:

○It is more common in equatorial Africa, Malawi, Uganda, and Cameroon, consistent with high malaria intensity.

○It is less common in sub-tropical regions of Africa or those countries at high altitude

○It is much less in Central and South America, Europe, and North America.

○It is least in Asia.

○2-4 times higher in males than females. The male:female ratio is highest before puberty and decreases with age.

○Inherited inborn errors of immunity or developmental disorders.

•Pathogenesis:

–The risk with malaria is correlated with the complexity of infection (mixed infection have a higher risk than single variant): Repeated infection results in chronic stimulation of B cells, suppression of T-cell immunity, and induction of  Activation- Induced cytidine Deaminase, an enzyme associated with the formation of the MYC translocation.

–EBV: Activation-Induced cytidine Deaminase activity and loss of T-cell responses to the EBV EBNA-1 protein leads to mutated rearranged IG genes with antigen selection

–HIV: Chronic antigen stimulation. It occurs at higher CD4 counts and is frequently the first presentation of HIV infection with a little effect of antiretroviral therapy.

–Post-transplantion: When the immunosuppressive medication is reduced and chronic immune stimulation is prolonged.

–TP53 mutation/deletion occur in 25- 50% of cases

•Clinical picture:

–Rapidly growing tumors due to the short doubling time 104

Original page 105

–Site-specific symptoms: Altered vision, nasal obstruction, enlarged tonsils, dental/jaw pain often with loss of teeth, abdominal masses (ileocecal lesions, retroperitoneal nodes), renal lesions, and testicular masses.

–Breast involvement is uncommon except in pregnant and lactating women, in whom the disease is usually bilateral.

–Lymphadenopathy mainly occurs in lymphoma arising in immune deficiency/dysregulation settings.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Leukemic presentation/bone marrow infiltration occurs in up to 20% of cases, especially if arising with immune deficiency/dysregulation, but is rare in endemic cases.

–Morphology:

○It has a diffuse growth pattern and is composed of monomorphic medium-sized lymphoid cells with basophilic cytoplasm, squared-off cytoplasmic borders, round nuclei with finely clumped and dispersed chromatin, and multiple basophilic paracentrally located nucleoli. Some cases show greater nuclear pleomorphism with more prominent and fewer nucleoli. Some cases show plasmacytoid differentiation with eccentric basophilic cytoplasm and often a single central nucleolus. Cells display some degree of cohesion, with abundant mitoses and apoptosis.

○Starry-sky: Sprinkling of tingible-body macrophages.

○Coagulative necrosis is common.

○Reactive small lymphocytes are rare. Some EBV-positive cases may have a florid granulomatous reaction obscuring the tumor. These cases are characterized by a pro-inflammatory microenvironment, typically present with limited stage disease, and have an especially good prognosis, sometimes even with spontaneous remission. 105

Original page 106

–Immunohistochemistry:

○Positive pan B-cell antigens (CD19, CD20, CD79a, CD22 and PAX5)

○Positive germinal center associated antigens (CD10 (particularly strong), BCL6, CD38, HGAL and MEF2B) with variable positivity of ET1, and negative LMO2

○Strong expression of IgM.

○Aberrant expression of CD43, LEF1 and TCL1A.

○Intense nuclear MYC expression in >80% cells. Lack of MYC expression would make the diagnosis not very likely

○Ki-67 expression is >95%.

○Cytoplasmic lipid vacuoles can be demonstrated by staining with adipophilin antibody.

○Negative CD5, CD23, CD138, BCL2, CD44 and TdT. However, weak BCL2 expression does not exclude the diagnosis. Strong expression of BCL2 and expression of cyclin D1 or TdT is not compatible with a diagnosis

–Flowcytometry:

○Dim CD45.

○Positive CD19, CD20, CD10, CD38, CD43, CD81, FMC-7

○Monotypic surface kappa or lambda light chain

○Bright CD38 and CD81

○Negative BCL2, CD44 and TdT.

–Genetic tests: Demonstration of MYC breakage or IG::MYC translocation, preferably with absence of BCL2 and BCL6 translocation, may support the diagnosis. Absence of IG::MYC fusion is against the diagnosis. 106

Original page 107

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Differential diagnosis:

–Diagnosis requires typical morphological features, characteristic phenotype (expression of CD20, CD10 and CD38; negative or very weak BCL2 expression; lack of CD44), intense MYC expression in >80% cells and a Ki-67 index of ≥95%.

–The differential diagnosis includes:

○Lymphoblastic lymphoma: Morphology (fine chromatin, scant cytoplasm), strong expression of TdT and positive markers of immaturity such as CD34.

○High-grade B-cell lymphoma, NOS: Negative CD10 and strong expression of BCL2.

○Dual rearrangements of MYC and BCL2 or BCL6 exclude the diagnosis of and are diagnosed as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements and DLBCL, NOS or High-grade B-cell lymphoma, NOS.

○High grade B-cell lymphoma with 11q aberration: Lack of MYC rearrangements and 11q gain/loss.

○Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma: Polygonal or spindle shape of some cells, prominent nucleoli, lack of deeply basophilic cytoplasm, and characteristic immunophenotypic expression of desmin and myogenin.

•Prognosis:

–Excellent prognosis in patients treated with contemporary immunochemotherapy regimens including rituximab in high-resource settings.

–In low/middle resource settings, prognosis is less good. 107
