Hodgkin lymphoma

Original page 116

•Cell of origin: Reed Sternberg cells and their mononuclear variants are derived from germinal center B-cells.

•Subtypes:

–Classic Hodgkin lymphoma

○Nodular sclerosis classic Hodgkin lymphoma

○Lymphocyte-rich classic Hodgkin lymphoma

○Mixed-cellularity classic Hodgkin lymphoma

○Lymphocyte depleted classic Hodgkin lymphoma

–Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma: Six different nodular and diffuse morphological patterns 116

Original page 117

•Definition: It is a neoplasm derived from germinal center B-cells, characterized by a low fraction of tumor cells embedded in a reactive micro-environment rich in immune cells.

•Subtypes:

○Nodular sclerosis classic Hodgkin lymphoma

○Lymphocyte-rich classic Hodgkin lymphoma

○Mixed-cellularity classic Hodgkin lymphoma

○Lymphocyte depleted classic Hodgkin lymphoma

•Epidemiology:

–Socioeconomic index: More with higher indices except the mixed cellularity subtype which is more in low-and-medium income countries

–Sex: Males is slightly more affected, except for the nodular sclerosis subtype which is slightly more in females.

–Age: Rare in children except the mixed cellularity subtype. It has a bimodal distribution in White and Asia/Pacific Islander populations (not in Black or Hispanic populations) with the first peak is 25-35 years and the second starts at 60 years.

–Other risk factors: Infectious mononucleosis, immunodeficiencies, including HIV/AIDS, geographic clustering and familial aggregation

•Etiology:

–EBV positive cases:

○Childhood cases are often EBV positive with increasing incidence with age due to the gradual declination of immune system.

○They are more with acquired immune-deficiency or solid-organ transplants after exclusion of immunodeficiency-associated lymphoproliferative disorders. 117

Original page 118

○They are strongly associated with HLA-A*01, an allele that cannot present EBV antigenic peptides, while HLA-A*02 is protective and can induce anti-EBV immune responses.

○Mixed cellularity and lymphocyte-depleted subtypes, are most frequently EBV positive.

–EBV-negative cases:

○There is a steady increasing incidenc and peak in middle age and a gradual decline in older age.

○They are most frequently of nodular sclerosis subtype.

–Genetic susceptibility: Familial clustering and high concordance in monozygotic twins.

•Pathogenesis:

–The Reed Sternberg cells are germinal center B cells with monoclonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangements and high load of somatic mutations. Hodgkin cells undergo incomplete cytokinesis yielding the multinucleated Reed Sternberg cells.

–Pathogenesis involves:

○Genomic alterations: Constitutive activation of oncogenic signaling pathways, in particular NF-kB and JAK/STAT:

➢Cytogenic abnormalities include gains of 2p13 (REL), 9p24.1 [CD274 (PDL1), PDCD1LG2 (PDL2), JAK2], 17q21 (MAP3K14), and loss of 6q23- q24 (TNFAIP3).

➢Somatic mutations include mutations of the NF-kB pathway (TNFAIP3, NFKBIA, NFKBIA, REL), the JAK/STAT pathway (SOCS1, PTPN1, STAT6, STAT3, CSF2RB), and regulators of immune escape such as inactivating mutations in the gene of the MHC class 1 component B2M, and the MHC class 2 transactivator. 118

Original page 119

○Crosstalk of neoplastic Reed Sternberg cells with the abundant tumor microenvironment: Reed Sternberg cells release a large array of chemokines (e.g., CCL17/TARC, CCL5), cytokines (e.g., IL5, IL7, IL13), and growth factors (M-CSF, FGF-2) to attract and modulate CD4+ regulatory and helper T cells, myeloid cells (eosinophils, macrophages, mast cells), and stromal cells (fibroblasts, mesenchymal stromal cells). These cells are not reactive to the neoplastic cells but rather promote cell survival, angiogenesis, and host-immune system evasion through:

➢The protective shield conferred by CD4+ T cell rosettes

➢Polarization of CD4+ T cells towards T regulatory cells

➢Monocyte differentiation into anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages and secretion of immunosuppressive cytokines (IL10, TGFβ).

○Latent EBV infection and immune evasion: EBV-infected Reed Sternberg cells show a latency type II program which includes expression of EBERs, EBNA1, LMP1 and LMP2A. The latter two are the main survival signals for germinal center B cells:

➢LMP1 is an oncogene and mimics an active CD40 receptor

➢LMP2A mimics B-cell receptor signaling.

•Clinical picture:

–Painless, firm peripheral lymphadenopathy, with characteristic contiguous nodal involvement.

–B symptoms.

–mediastinal disease may cause persistent cough, shortness of breath, or even superior vena cava syndrome.

–Pruritus: Less frequent

–Alcohol-induced pain of affected lymph node regions: Rare, but characteristic.

–Paraneoplastic phenomena including autoimmune hemolysis, ichthyosis, neuropathy, and cerebellar: Infrequent 119

Original page 120

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–CBC: Anemia, leukocytosis with neutrophilia and lymphocytopenia

–Elevated C-reactive protein.

–Microscopy: Mononuclear Hodgkin cells and bi- or multinucleated Reed Sternberg cells within a characteristic cellular microenvironment:

○Reed Sternberg cells: Four to five times the size of background lymphocytes and have large nuclei with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli surrounded by a perinuclear halo giving the classic owl eye appearance

○Hodgkin cells: Round nucleus with a prominent nucleolus.

○Lacunar cells: In nodular sclerosis classic Hodgkin lymphoma

○Mummified cells (apoptotic forms): Dense cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei

○Microenvironment (non-neoplastic): Lymphocytes in most cases are T cells accompanied by variable numbers of eosinophils, histiocytes, neutrophils and plasma cells. The lymphocyte-rich subtype may include abundant reactive B cells of mantle cell type.

○Epithelioid granulomas may be focal, or may sometimes dominate the pictureand may be mistaken as mycobacterial disease

○Subtypes:

➢Nodular sclerosis subtype:

❖Sclerotic bands that surround one to several nodules containing Reed Sternberg cells and the reactive infiltrate with no capsular fibrosis.

❖Lacunar cells are characteristic and result from retraction of the cytoplasm during fixation, resulting in the appearance of neoplastic cells residing in holes or lacunae.

❖Reed Sternberg cells are common

❖Hodgkin cells with pleomorphic morphology can be seen.

❖Syncytial variant: Numerous neoplastic cells in sheets. 120

Original page 121

❖The inflammatory infiltrate comprises eosinophils, histiocytes, small lymphocytes, and occasionally neutrophils.

❖Necrosis.

➢Mixed-cellularity subtype :

❖Reed Sternberg cells are relatively frequent and diffusely scattered

❖Mixed inflammatory infiltrate: Small lymphocytes, histiocytes, eosinophils and plasma cells.

❖Epithelioid histiocytes or granulomas especially in EBV-positive cases.

❖Fibrosis: Finely reticular with no fibrous septa or capsular fibrosis.

➢Lymphocyte rich subtype: It may be confused with nodular lymphocyte predominant type:

❖Nodular, or less commonly, diffuse infiltration by abundant small lymphocytes with lack of neutrophils and eosinophils (may present in small numbers and are located in the interfollicular zones).

❖Reed Sternberg cells are predominantly found within the nodules but consistently outside of the germinal centers.  Some Reed Sternberg cells resemble lymphocyte predominant cells or mononuclear lacunar cells.

❖In diffuse cases, the small lymphocytes of the cellular background may be admixed with histiocytes with or without epithelioid features.

➢Lymphocyte depleted subtype (rare): It is strongly associated with EBV:

❖Diffuse growth pattern.

❖Predominance of pleomorphic Reed Sternberg cell with few background lymphocytes.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Positive CD30 and CD15 in a membranous pattern, with accentuation in the Golgi area of the cytoplasm. CD15 may also be expressed in a cytoplasmic granular or focal pattern. CD30 expression is uniform across the cell.

○Negative CD45 121

Original page 122

○Negative for J chain, Ig heavy and light chains, CD68R, CD19 and CD79a. The B-cell nature of Reed Sternberg cells is demonstrated by PAX5 which is weaker than that of reactive B cells. Occasionally, both light chains are positive in the same cell with negative mRNA due to absorption from the tissue extracellular matrix free protein

○CD20 may be detectable in some cases on few neoplastic cells with varied intensity.

○The expression of B-cell transcription factors such as OCT2, BOB1, PU1 and BCL6 is downregulated in most cases but are more expressed in the lymphocyte rich subtype. The transcription factor MUM1 is strongly positive in Reed Sternberg cells with negative CD138.

○Germinal center cell markers are rarely expressed except for BCL6 (weak positive).

○Aberrant expression of one or more T-cell antigens

○Positive proliferation-associated nuclear antigens, such as PCNA or MIB1.

○Nuclear expression of GATA3

○PDL1 is strong positive in some cases

○Positive fascin

○CD23 is negative in most cases

○Nuclear expression of STAT6YE361, with or without cytoplasmic staining

○The background small lymphoid cells:

➢They include both B cells and T cells.

➢B-cells are more in the lymphocyte rich subtype and fewer in the lymphocyte depleted subtype.

➢The rosettes around the Reed Sternberg cells are usually CD4+ Tcells

➢The lymphocyte rich subtype: Small B cells in the represent expanded mantle zones (positive for IgM and IgD). The follicular architecture of B-cell nodules is highlighted by a dense meshwork of CD21+ follicular dendritic 122

Original page 123

cells. Rosettes with PD1+ T-cells (T follicular helper cells) surround the neoplastic cells in nearly one-half of cases.

○Background cells include CD15 positive eosinophils and neutrophils and CD163/CD68 positive macrophages.

–EBV infection:

○In-situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER).

○Reed Sternberg cells express EBV latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1) and EBNA1 without EBNA2 (type II EBV latency).

–Genetic tests:

○TCR clonality assays can be helpful in excluding peripheral T cell lymphoma

○9p24/ CD274/ PDCD1LG2 copy number status is predictive of response to checkpoint inhibition therapy.

•Differential Diagnosis:

–T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B cell lymphoma:  It has a background rich in histiocytes and small lymphocytes but large neoplastic cells, have a full B-cell immunophenotyping with positive BCL6, negative CD15 and CD30 and negative EBV.

–Infectious mononucleosis:  Many immunoblasts in a background of smaller lymphocytes and plasma cells.  Some immunoblasts may resemble Reed Sternberg cells but most large cells have classic features of immunoblasts with polytypic kappa and lambda light chains.  Reed Sternberg -like cells are CD45 positive, CD20 positive, CD30 positive, CD15 negative and EBER positive. The background small lymphoid cells are mostly CD8 positive T cells (CD4 positive in classic Hodgkin lymphoma). Smaller cells are EBV positive (EBV positive Reed Sternberg cells in classic Hodgkin lymphoma).

–EBV positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: It lacks the eosinophils and rosette formation by T cells and shows typical B-cell immunophenotyping with lack of CD15. 123

Original page 124

–Mediastinal grey zone lymphoma: Mediastinal localization with typical B-cell immunophenotyping and sheets of neoplastic cells

–Immune deficiency/dysregulation-associated lymphoproliferative disorders: Detailed clinical evaluation, staging and information on medical history.

–Nodal TFH cell lymphoma, angioimmunoblastic type (nTFHL-AI) and other nodal TFH cell lymphomas: Typical B-cell immunophenotyping with frequently expressed light chains. Few cases show the typical immunophenotyping of Reed Sternberg cells. The rosett is formed by neoplastic T-cells of TFH phenotype and are often accompanied by an increase in more typical B-immunoblasts. Neoplastic cells are positive for RHOA  (G17V) and IDH2 (R172) mutations.

–Peripheral T cell lymphoma, NOS, and anaplastic large cell lymphoma: Neoplastic T-cells. ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma are PAX5 negative.

–Hodgkin-like adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma

–Hodgkin-like lymphoproliferations in draining lymph nodes of CD30-positive primary cutaneous lymphoproliferative diseases: Lack of expression of PAX5

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Most patients can be cured with modern polychemotherapy, selectively combined with radiotherapy. 124

toc: Plasma cell neoplasms and other diseases with paraproteins
sections.html:
Original page 125

•Definition: It is a germinal center-derived B-cell neoplasm composed of scattered large neoplastic B cells with multilobated nuclei (lymphocyte predominant orLP cells) within nodules dominated by mantle zone B cells and follicular dendritic cells.

•Subtypes: Six different nodular and diffuse morphological patterns are recognized.

•Etiology:

–Unknown.

–Familial cases are rare and are associated with germline NPAT mutations or TET2 haploinsufficiency

–It is associated with primary immunodeficiency syndromes, such as Hermansky- Pudlak syndrome type 2 and autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.

–IgD-positive cases are more frequently of HLA haplotypes HLA-DRB1*04 and HLA-DRB1*07, indicating a role for cognate T-cell help.

–EBV plays no significant role.

•Pathogenesis:

–The LP precursor cells may enter germinal centers, undergo clonal selection and malignant transformation due to aberrant somatic hypermutation.

–BCL6 translocations or amplifications are common.

–Some cases are triggered by preceding bacterial infections, resulting in an extensive immune reaction in susceptible patients.

–IgD-positive cases show additive stimulation by Moraxella-derived antigen and super-antigen.

–There is a close interaction between LP cells and rosetting PD1-positive T cells via immunological synapses.

•Clinical picture:

–Age is higher in women than men and cases with IgD-positive LP cells occurs are more in young men. 125

Original page 126

–Lymphadenopathy: Cervical, axillary, iliac and inguinal regions.

–Bulky disease and advanced stage IV defining organ involvement are less than in classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Morphology:

○Neoplastic LP cells are large with multilobated nuclei with one or more nucleoli and pale cytoplasm (often resembling popcorn).

○The immune microenvironment is composed of many non-neoplastic B cells, T cells, often with activated morphological features including clear cytoplasm and a more open chromatin structure, and histiocytes, including epithelioid histiocytes. Histiocytes may cluster or form granulomas around nodules. Neutrophils and eosinophils are absent.

○Sclerosis is uncommon at diagnosis but often present at recurrence.

–Immunohistochemistry:

○Positive expression of B-cell markers (CD20, CD79a, OCT2, BOB1, PU-1). OCT2 is the most reliable positive marker and CD79a only rarely shows weaker expression. CD20 and one or more of the B cell transcription factors (BOB1, OCT2, PU-1) may be lost in rare cases. CD19 is frequently negative.

○Germinal center B-cell markers such as BCL6, LMO2 and HGAL are positive in the vast majority, but CD10 is negative.

○The LP cells are usually negative for CD30 and rarely positive for CD15. IgD is typically expressed in LP cells in especially with extranodular tumor cells and mild cytologic atypia of background T-cells. EBV is rarely positive in LP cells. mef2b is expressed in LP cells, while STAT6 is negative. 126

Original page 127

○Background small B cells have a mantle zone phenotype (IgD-positive, germinal center markers negative) are associated with expanded CD21+, CD23+ follicular dendritic cell meshworks.

○T-follicular helper (TFH) cells, which express CD3, PD1, CD57, BCL6, CXCL13 and ICOS, are abundant forming rosettes encircling LP cells.

–Genetic tests: LP cells are clonal by single-cell PCR analyses.

•Prognosis:

–Risk factors for relapse: Variant histopathological growth patterns, male gender and low serum albumin level. Variant growth patterns correlate with shorter time-to-relapse .

–Risk factors for transformation to large B-cell lymphoma: Infradiaphragmatic and splenic involvement, and clonal IG rearrangement

•Diagnostic criteria:

127

Plasma cell neoplasms and other diseases with paraproteins

Original page 128

•Definition: These are mature B-cell neoplasms or plasma cell neoplasms producing paraproteins or M-proteins, which are either monoclonal intact immunoglobulins, light chains or occasionally heavy chains or misfolded immunoglobulins

•They include:

–Monoclonal gammopathies

–Diseases with monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition

–Heavy chain disease

–Plasma cell neoplasms 128

Monoclonal gammopathies

Original page 129

•They include:

–Cold agglutinin disease

–IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance

–Non-IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance

–Monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance 129

Original page 130

•Definition: It is an autoimmune hemolytic anemia mediated by monoclonal B- cell proliferation which produces autoantibodies that agglutinate erythrocytes 0 at an optimum temperature of 0-4C in the absence of any infection or lymphoma.

•Epidemiology:

–Rare, but four-fold higher in colder countries.

–Slightly more frequent in females

–Median age in the late 60s.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis:

–Genetic changes

○Clonal rearrangements of immunoglobulin heavy and light chain genes.

○Somatic mutation of the immunoglobulin genes.

○Cytogenetic changes: Gains of chromosomes 12 or 18 (70%).

○Mutation of multiple regions within the IG genes increasing the specific binding of the I antigen, leading to more severe anemia.

○Mutation of KMT2D and CARD11.

○No MYD88 p.L265P mutation.

–Agglutination The IgM monoclonal pentameric autoantibodies bind to the I 0 antigen on the red blood cell surface at an optimum temperature of 0-4C.

–Extravascular hemolysis: The bound IgM triggers the classic complement pathway.

–Intravascular hemolysis: Activation of the terminal complement cascade.

•Clinical picture: Cold-induced symptoms as acrocyanosis, Raynaud phenomenon, livedo reticularis due to red blood cell agglutination. 130

Original page 131

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Anemia with extravascular or intravascular hemolysis

–Blood film: Red blood cell agglutination, anisocytosis, and polychromasia.

–A small serum monoclonal IgM paraprotein, mostly kappa.

–Bone marrow aspirate: Increased erythropoiesis.

–Bone marrow biopsy: Small lymphoid cells with round to slightly oval nuclei, homogeneous dark chromatin pattern and scanty clear cytoplasm forming nodular aggregates and sparse interstitial infiltration. Mature plasma cells <5%.

131

Original page 132

•Diagnostic criteria:

132

sections.t: IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
sections.html:
Original page 133

•Definition: Presence of a serum monoclonal protein of < 3g/dl and <10% bone marrow clonal B cells and plasma cells infiltration, with no evidence of anemia, constitutional symptoms, hyperviscosity, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly that can be attributed to the underlying lymphoproliferative disorder.

•Epidemiology:

–20% of all MGUS.

–The incidence increases with age.

–Higher in males than females, and in black people compared with whites.

–First degree relatives may have a higher risk.

•Clinical picture: Asymptomatic.

•Complications:

–Progression to Waldenström macroglobulinemia or immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis

–Rare progression to IgM plasma cell myeloma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, or other lymphomas.

–IgM-related peripheral neuropathy, and Schnitzler syndrome (Rare chronic urticarial).

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Bone marrow: < 10% clonal involvement by lymphoplasmacytoid or plasma cell neoplastic cells.

–Immunophenotyping: sIgM+, CD5+/−, CD10−, CD19+, CD20+ and CD23−

–Genetic tests: MYD88 p.L265P mutation may be found.

•Diagnostic criteria:

133

sections.t: Non-IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
sections.html:
Original page 134

•Definition: Presence of IgG, IgA, or rarely IgE, IgD or light chain serum monoclonal protein of < 3g/dl, < 10%, and absence of end-organ damage such as hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, and bone lesions that can be attributed to the plasma cell proliferative disorder.

•Light chain MGUS: It is a subtype of MGUS characterized by abnormal serum free chain (<0.26 or >1.65) and increased level of the involved light chain with no immunoglobulin heavy chain expression on immunofixation, and absence of end-organ damage that can be attributed to the plasma cell proliferative disorder.

•Subtypes: IgG, IgA, IgD, IgE and Light chain MGUS

•Epidemiology:

–80% of all MGUS.

–The incidence increases with age.

–Higher in males than females, and in black people compared with whites.

–First degree relatives may have a higher risk.

•Etiology: Unknown, but there is a higher risk with family history, obesity, exposure to pesticides, and with immunosuppression.

•Pathogenesis:

–It occurs as a result of antigenic stimulation of plasma cells.

–Cytogenetic abnormalities: Hyperdiploidy and immunoglobulin heavy chain rearrangement with 11q13 (CCND1), 4p16.3 (FGFR3 and NSD2), 6p21 (CCND3), 16q23 (MAF), and 20q11 (MAFB).

–The second-hit is responsible for progression of MGUS.

•Clinical picture: Asymptomatic. 134

Original page 135

•Complications:

–Progression to plasma cell myeloma, plasmacytoma, or immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis.

–Proliferative glomerulonephritis

–Dermatologic diseases such as lichen myxedematosus, necrobiotic xanthogranuloma, scleromyxedema, and pyoderma gangrenosum

–Rarely: Peripheral neuropathy.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Bone marrow: < 10% involvement by clonal mature plasma cells.

–Immunophenotyping: CD38+, CD45 dim to negative, CD19-, and CD138+.

–Genetic tests: t(11;14), t(4;14) or t(14;16) with hyperdiploidy (trisomies of chromosome 7, 9, 11, 15, 19).

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Abnormal serum free light chain ratio, IgA or IgM type MGUS, and serum M-protein value >1.5 g/dL is considered high risk. 135

Original page 136

•Definition: It is a plasma cell or B-cell neoplasm that does not meet the accepted criteria of malignancy but secretes a monoclonal immunoglobulin or fragment resulting in kidney injury. N.B.: Renal impairment secondary to light chain cast nephropathy in plasma cell neoplasm, is a multiple myeloma / plasma cell myeloma defining event.

•Epidemiology:

–MGRS represents a subset of patients with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, smoldering malignancies and clonal B-cell proliferation that does not meet the diagnostic criteria for lymphoma. The true prevalence is unknown but may be close to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. The median age at diagnosis is around 60 years of age but disease can occur in the late teens and early 20s. There is a male predominance of 60% to 75%.

•Etiology:

–A plasma cell neoplasm is the most common cause of immunoglobulin associated amyloidosis, monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease, light chain proximal tubulopathy, crystal-storing histiocytosis, crystalglobulin induced nephropathy, C3 glomerulopathy with monoclonal gammopathy and thrombotic microangiopathy. B-cell clones are the most common cause of cryoglobulinemia secondary to monoclonal gammopathy. In proliferative glomerulonephritis with monoclonal immunoglobulin deposits, a plasma cell neoplasm makes up 50% of the cases while CD20+ B-cell neoplasms account for the other half where one-third of the neoplasms co-express CD20 and CD38.

•Pathogenesis: Injure of the kidney either by deposition, vascular occlusion, or activation of complement. 136

Original page 137

•Clinical picture:

–The clinical presentation of MGRS is broad and encompasses variable combinations of proteinuria, haematuria, acute or chronic renal insufficiency, hypertension, and hypocomplementemia. Microscopic haematuria and hypertension are common, but hypotension is common in patients with immunoglobulin associated amyloidosis. The severity of proteinuria or renal impairment depends on the kidney lesion. Patients with immunoglobulin-associated amyloidosis, monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease and cryoglobulinemia often have extrarenal manifestations including congestive heart failure, autonomic/peripheral neuropathy, liver failure, and skin rash/purpura.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Macroscopic appearance Not relevant Histopathology Refer to the sections on monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. Cytology Refer to the sections on monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. Diagnostic molecular pathology Refer to the sections on monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance.

•Diagnostic criteria:

137

Original page 138

138

Diseases with monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition

Original page 139

–Immunoglobulin-related (AL) amyloidosis

–Monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease

•Definition: It is defined as extracellular deposition of immunoglobulin light chain derived linear non-branching fibrils (with a width of 9 nm) produced by clonal plasma cells or B-cells causing progressive end organ dysfunction.

•Subtypes:

–Systemic AL amyloidosis

–Localized AL amyloidosis

–Heavy chain Amyloidosis

•Epidemiology: 1/6 as common as plasma cell myeloma.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: Unstable immunoglobulin light chain (or fragments) interacts with the extracellular environment leading to proteolytic cleavage, and binding to matrix components such as glycosaminoglycans, serum amyloid P and collagen that facilitate aggregation.

•Clinical picture:

–Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and thickened ventricular walls.

–Peripheral neuropathy

–Hepatomegaly.

–Autonomic dysfunction

–Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome

–Macroglossia, submandibular swelling and periorbital purpura.

–Non-specific symptoms: fatigue, edema, weight loss, and dyspnea 139

Original page 140

–Serum free light chains: Elevated and/or an abnormal free light chain ratio in two thirds of cases, suggesting that they may be minimally secretory or oligosecretory.

–Non-producer myeloma: 15% of cases who have no cytoplasmic immunoglobulin.

–Normal immunoglobulins: Minimally reduced.

–The immunophenotyping and genetics prognostic factors are similar to those of other types of plasma cell myeloma.

•Plasma cell leukemia: It is a plasma cell myeloma in which clonal plasma cells constituting more than 20% of total leukocytes in the blood or plasma absolute count 9 is more than 2.0 x 10/L. Clinical picture:

–Lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, and renal failure are more common,

–Lytic bone lesions and bone pain are less common. Laboratory diagnosis: I-Blood film: 9

–Plasma cells are more than 20% or more than 2X 10/L.

–Blue background.

–Increased roleoux. 2-ESR: Very high. 176

Original page 177

3-Biochemical tests: High serum calcium, creatinineandtotal protein and low serum albumin. 4-Serum and urine protein electrophoresis: Monoclonal band. 5-Immunofixation: M protein is more common to be light chain only, IgD or IgE than lgG or lgA. 6-Immunophenotyping:

–CD19(-), and surface Ig(-) but it is assigned to B cell lineage because it is CD79a(+) and cytoplasmic Ig(+).

–Light chain restriction.

–CD38(+), CD138(+) and CD10(+).

–CD20 expression is more frequent than other types of plasma cell myeloma.

–CD56 is negative in about 80% of cases.

7-Genetic tests:

–It has a higher incidence of the high-risk genetic findings.

–The t(11 ;14) translocation is over-represented in primary cases with a more favorable prognosis. 7-Bone marrow: Extensive and diffuse infiltration of the bone marrow. 8-Extramedullary organs as liver, spleen, body cavity effusion and spinal fluid: There may be infiltration by the neoplastic plasma cells. 177

Original page 178

•Definition and subtypes: This is a group of rare paraneoplastic syndromes associated with plasma cell neoplasms, as follows:

–POEMS syndrome (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy and skin changes)

–TEMPI syndrome (telangiectasia, elevated erythropoietin and erythrocytosis, monoclonal gammopathy, perinephric fluid collection and intrapulmonary shunting)

–AESOP syndrome (adenopathy and extensive skin patch overlying plasmacytoma).

•Etiology and pathogenesis:

–Unknown. Levels of VEGF correlate with disease activity in POEMS but may not be a driving force of the disease

–Cytokines (e.g., IL-1b, TNF-a, IL-6) and inflammatory and vascular growth factors (e.g., VEGF) secreted from the plasma cells and platelets.

–Cytogenetic abnormalities in POEMS syndrome are similar to other plasma cell neoplasms with no 17p deletions and with a low prevalence of hyperdiploidy and 14q32 rearrangements.

–No recurrent genetic abnormalities in TEMPI syndrome.

•Clinical picture:

–POEMS syndrome:

○Polyneuropathy: Subacute, distal, symmetrical, sensorimotor neuropathy.

○Osteosclerosis of pelvis, thoracic and lumbar vertebrae, and ribs, and less commonly in the scapula, clavicle, sternum, skull, and long bones. 178

Original page 179

○Organomegally: Hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy.

○Endocrinopathy: Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism,

○Skin: Hyperpigmentation, hemangiomas and nail changes.

○Others: Papilledema, volume overload, acrocyanosis, weight loss, clubbing, hyperhidrosis, pulmonary hypertension/restrictive lung disease, thrombotic diatheses, diarrhea and low vitamin B12 values.

–TEMPI syndrome:

○Telangiectasias: On the face, upper back, chest and hands, whereas the lower extremities are spared.

○Erythrocytosis: Unexplained erythrocytosis progresses to secondary polycythemia.

○Perinephric fluid collections.

–AESOP syndrome:

○Solitary plasmacytoma.

○Skin patches: Slow-growing red, brown or violaceous with visible blood vessels on the thorax. They are variable in size with fine desquamation especially at the edge, smaller satellite lesions may be observed.

○Polyneuropathy

○Lymphadenopathy: Unilateral /bilateral typically

○Some patients develop organomegaly, and endocrinopathy.

•Laboratory findings:

–POEMS syndrome:

○M protein is IgA or IgG/ lambda with a level below plasma cell myeloma levels.

○N-terminal propeptide of type I collagen (P1NP), a marker for osteosclerotic metastasis is markedly elevated. 179

Original page 180

○Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF): Markedly elevated in plasma and serum and correlate with disease severity.

○Peripheral blood smears are normal

○Bone marrow:

➢Clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow (usually < 5%and atypical with sclerosis of the bony lamellae) or less commonly solitary or multiple plasmacytomas.

➢Reactive lymphoid aggregates with plasma cell rimming.

➢Megakaryocyte hyperplasia, clustering and atypia with small mono- and hypolobated nuclei, hyperchromatic nuclei, nuclear segmentation, and/or larger forms.

○Immunophenotyping: Similar to other plasma cell neoplasms mostly with lambda-restriction.

–TEMPI syndrome:

○Serum erythropoietin levels exceed most other causes of erythrocytosis.

○No JAK2 mutations.

○Monoclonal gammopathy: IgG kappa

○VEGF levels are not elevated.

○Elevated level of MIF (macrophage migration inhibitory factor)

○Bone marrow is unremarkable:

➢Erythroid hyperplasia

➢Mild atypia in erythroid cells and megakaryocytes.

➢Few monoclonal plasma cells 180

Original page 181

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis of POEMS syndrome: It is chronic and progressive with a good outcome with radiation, chemotherapy and stem cell transplantation. 181

Original page 187

–Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease: It is a self-limiting disorder characterized by lymphadenopathy with paracortical proliferation of immunoblasts, infiltration by histiocytes with characteristic nuclear features, and apoptosis or necrosis with abundant nuclear debris.

–Indolent T-lymphoblastic proliferation: It is an extra-thymic non-clonal expansion of T lymphoblasts occurring alone or in association with other disorders, including Castleman disease and others.

187

Original page 188

–Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome: Itis an inborn or acquired error of immunity characterized by lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias, and increased risk of lymphoma. It is associated with germline or somatic defects in the FAS-mediated apoptosis pathway and the accumulation of CD4/CD8 double negative αβ-T cells

188

Precursor T cell neoplasms

Original page 189

–T-lymphoblastic leukemia / lymphoma, NOS

–Early T-precursor lymphoblastic leukemia / lymphoma 189

Original page 190

•Definition: It is an acute neoplasm characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of T lymphoblasts and their infiltration of peripheral blood and bone marrow as the primary site of involvement (leukemia) or infiltration of lymph nodes, thymus or other extra-nodal sites as the primary involvement (lymphoma N.B.: The distinction becomes arbitrary when both marrow and non-marrow sites are involved, although many treatment protocols use >25% marrow blasts to define leukemia.

•Epidemiology:

–15% of childhood ALL and more common in adolescents than in younger children (25% of adult ALL)

–More common in males.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis:

–Multistep accumulation of genetic/epigenetic alterations in oncogenic and tumor suppressors pathways:

○Mutations affecting the NOTCH1 pathway

○Translocations of transcription factors to chromosomal regions of TCR loci

○Mutations in epigenetic regulators (EZH2, SUZ12, and EED) and chromatin modifiers (PHF6, KDM6A, and USP7).

○Mutation of genes involved in the JAK-STAT signaling pathway (IL7R, JAK1, JAK3, and STAT5B), PI3K-AKT signaling pathways (PI3K and PTEN), RAS-MAPK signaling pathways (HRAS, KRAS, and PTPN11)

○Deletions in cell cycle regulatory genes (CDKN2A, CDKN2B, CDKN1B, RB1, CCDN2, CCND3, CTCF, and MYB).

–Ribosomal dysfunction 190

Original page 191

–Deregulated expression of oncogenic miRNAs or long non-coding RNAs related to T-cell development. N.B.: T-ALL in monozygotic twins shares the same TR gene rearrangement, suggesting an in utero origin of the earliest genetic lesions.

•Clinical picture:

–Rapidly growing large mediastinal or other tissue mass.

–Lymphadenopathy

–Hepatosplenomegaly.

–Pleural/pericardial effusions

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–CBC: High leukocyte count

–Bone marrow:

○Relative sparing of normal bone marrow hematopoiesis compared to B-ALL.

○Biopsy: Infiltration displaces normal marrow elements, and show high N:C ratio, thin nuclear membranes, finely stippled chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli.

–Morphology: Blasts have scant basophilic agranular or rarely vacuolated cytoplasm, round to irregular or convoluted nuclei, and range from small to medium size with a high N:C ratio with condensed chromatin and no evident nucleoli, to larger blasts with finely dispersed chromatin and relatively prominent nucleoli. Occasionally, they resemble more mature lymphocytes.

–Cytochemistry:

○Negative MPO

○It may stain light grey and weakly with Sudan Black B when granules are present.

○Sodium fluoride sensitive non-specific esterase may show multifocal punctate or Golgi staining.

○Periodic acid-Schiff may show coarse heavy cytoplasmic staining. 191

Original page 192

–Immunophenotyping:

○cCD3: Positive

○CD7: Uniform and higher than mature T cells, but may be lower.

○CD5: Lower than mature T cells

○CD2: Positive.

○CD45: Lower than mature lymphocytes, although not as low as is common in B-ALL/LBL.

○Markers of immaturity: CD1a, CD34 (1/3 of cases), CD117 and/or CD99 in addition to TdT.

○There are four immunophenotypic subtypes:

➢Pro-T / T-I ad Pre-T / T-II: Many cases now meet the criteria for early T precursor ALL: CD4 and CD8 are frequently coexpressed, often with CD1a, and CD10 may be positive

➢Cortical T / T-III

➢Medullary T / T-IV: It expresses either CD4 or CD8, usually with sCD3.

○Nuclear staining for TAL1 may be positive

○LMO2: Positive.

○CD56: Positive in some cases.

○CD79a/ CD19/ CD13/ CD33/ CD117  may be positive in few cases

○HLA-DR is negative.

–Genetic tests:

○Clonal rearrangements of the TCRB and/or TCRG genes: It may be used to monitor residual disease.

○Recurrent cytogenetic abnormality: Rearrangements of alpha and delta TCR loci at 14q11.2, the beta locus at 7q34, and the gamma locus at 7p14.1, with:

➢T-lineage transcription factors TLX1, TLX3, TAL1, TAL2, LMO1, LMO2, LYL1, NKX2-1,2,5, OLIG2, and HOXA. 192

Original page 193

➢Other transcription factors include MYC and MYB, and the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase LCK.

➢Other important rearrangements in T-ALL involve MLLT10, KMT2A, ABL1, and NUP98. T-ALL is divided into eight genetic subgroups based aberrant expression of:

❖TAL

❖TAL2

❖TLX1: Relatively favorable prognosis

❖TLX3

❖HOXA

❖LMO1/LMO2

❖LMO2/LYL1

❖NKX2-1.

○Deletions:

➢9p: Loss of the tumor suppressor gene CDKN2A

➢BCL11B, LEF1, WT1, NF1 ETV6, RUNX1, and GATA3.

○Signaling pathway deregulation: NOTCH1, PI3K-AKT, JAK-STAT, RASMAPK, and ABL kinase pathways.

○Epigenetic dysregulation: Mutations in PHF6, SUZ12, EZH2, TET2, H3F3A, KDM6A, EED, SETD2, and DNMT3A.

•Diagnostic criteria:

193

Original page 194

•Differential diagnosis:

–Lymphocyte rich Thymoma, thymic hyperplasia and ectopic thymus: Larger epithelial cells with low mitotic activity and more vesicular chromatin are usually present. Immunohistochemical staining highlights the keratin positive epithelial cells in an “interlocking” pattern reminiscent of normal thymic architecture. Lymphoid cells demonstrate normal thymocyte maturational patterns when analyzed by flowcytometry, skewed toward the common thymocyte maturational stage, which along with polyclonal TCR gene rearrangements can be helpful in diagnosis.

–Other subtypes of acute leukemia including their extramedullary presentations: Distinction is facilitated by flowcytometry.

–ETP-ALL: Expression of one or more of the myeloid/stem markers such as CD13, CD33, CD34, CD117 or HLA-DR, an absence of CD1a and CD8, and decreased to absent CD5

–MPAL, T/Myeloid: Absence of cytoplasmic MPO and lack of monocytic differentiation.

–Acute Undifferentiated Leukemia: Lack of cytoplasmic CD3 expression.

–Cases with a significant eosinophilic component or associated myeloproliferative features may represent Myeloid/Lymphoid Neoplasms with Eosinophilia and Defining Gene. Molecular testing is required to establish the diagnosis.

–Some cases shows surface CD3 expression and distinction from mature T cell lymphoma is based on a combination of morphology, immunophenotypic profile and molecular genetics. Mature T cell lymphoma/leukemia lacks immature antigens, e.g. CD34, TdT or CD1a and typically shows dimmer CD7 expression. Detection of NOTCH1 mutation favors T-ALL whereas TCL1 expression or rearrangement supports T-PLL. 194

Original page 195

–NK-ALL: Negative sCD3 and positive CD2, CD7, CD5, cytoplasmic CD3 (ζ and ε chains) and CD56. No clonal TCR rearrangement.

–Indolent T lymphoblastic proliferations: Polyclonal proliferations of T lymphoblasts in extrathymic sites, primarily in lymph nodes. Flowcytometry demonstrates a variety of normal T maturational stages and LMO2 is negative by immunohistochemistry.

•Prognosis:

–Prognosis is better than that of B-ALL. Long-term response: 85% in children and adolescents, and 60% in adults. Outcomes of relapsed cases is poor

–The most significant predictor of outcome: minimal residual disease at the end of consolidation

–The prognosis of T-lymphoblastic lymphoma depends on age, stage, and lactate dehydrogenase levels. 195

Original page 196

•Definition: It is a neoplasm composed of blasts committed to the T-cell lineage with a unique immunophenotype that includes expression of stem cell markers and/or myeloid lineage markers.

•Epidemiology:

–12-17% of pediatric T-ALL and 22-40% of adult T-ALL.

–In the adults, patients tend to be older in comparison to non-ETP-ALL.

•Etiology:

–Unknown in most cases.

–Germline RUNX1 variants

–Mutated JAK3.

•Pathogenesis:

–Cell of origin: The earliest recognizable stage in T-cell ontogeny, characterized by multilineage differentiation potential and expression of lymphoid, myeloid and stem cell markers

–Leukemic cells express plasticity, with both stem cell and T-cell signatures.

–Leukemic cells can differentiate to stimulate an immunosuppressive microenvironment through expression of the LGALS9 checkpoint molecule and support of dysfunctional CD8-positive T-cells.

–Increased expression of MEF2C and decreased expression of BCL11B and GATA3.

–EZH2 and RUNX1 inactivating mutations as initiating events leading to expansion of early thymic progenitors with further acquisition of mutations (e.g. FLT3) resulting in constitutive activation of the RAS signaling pathway.

–Activating mutations in genes regulating cytokine receptor and RAS signaling (FLT3, NRAS, KRAS, IL7R, JAK3, JAK1, SH2B3 and BRAF), hematopoietic 196

Original page 197

development (GATA3, ETV6, RUNX1, IKZF1), and histone modifications (EZH2, EED, SUZ12, SETD2, EP300).

–NOTCH1 mutations are uncommon

–CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion is uncommon.

–No TRG gene rearrangement.

•Clinical picture:

–Symptoms and signs related to cytopenias

–Manifestations of extramedullary disease.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–CBC: The white blood count may or may not be elevated.

–Morphology: Lymphoblasts are small to medium size, with round to convoluted nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin, small or absent nucleoli, and mildly to moderately basophilic cytoplasm.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Expression of cytoplasmic CD3. Surface CD3 is usually absent.

○<5% of blasts are positive for CD1a and CD8

○<75% of blasts are positive for CD5 (Dim CD5 can be also defined as mean fluorescent intensity that is at least 1 log less than that of normal T cells provided that the mean fluorescent intensity of T cells is at least two logs greater than that of negative control)

○≥25% of blasts are positive for 1 or more myeloid (CD11b, CD13, CD33, CD65, CD117) and/or stem cell (CD34, HLA-DR) markers.

○CD7 is consistently positive

○<10% of blasts are positive for myeloperoxidase by flowcytometry, and < 3% of blasts are positive for myeloperoxidase by cytochemistry N.B.: T-ALL cases with an immunophenotype similar to ETP-ALL but with CD5 expression on ≥75% of blasts are called near-ETP-ALL. 197

Original page 198

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Differential diagnosis: Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia: In ETP-ALL, <10% of blasts are positive for myeloperoxidase by flowcytometry, and < 3% of blasts are positive for myeloperoxidase by cytochemistry

•Prognosis: Long-term outcomes despite higher rates of MRD-positive disease post induction due to treatment intensification for MRD-positive patients and the increased rate of allogeneic stem cell transplantation after first remission. 198

Mature T cell Neoplasms

Original page 199

•Definition: They are clonal malignancies characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of mature T lymphoid cells.

•Classes:

–T-Prolymphocytic leukemia

–T-large granular lymphocytic leukemia

–NK-large granular lymphocytic leukemia (NK-LGLL)

–Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma

–Sezary syndrome

–Aggressive NK-cell leukemia. 199

Original page 200

•Definition: It is a clonal proliferation of small to medium-sized prolymphocytes with a mature post-thymic T-cell phenotype characterized by juxtaposition of the TCL1A or MTCP1 gene next to a TCR locus mostly the TRA/TRD locus.

•Epidemiology:

–It is rare accounting for 2% of mature lymphoid neoplasms in adults >30 years.

–It predominates in the elderly

–There is a slight male predominance (1.33).

•Etiology: Unknown but may arise in the cases of Ataxia-Telangiectasia with germline mutations in the ATM gene.

•Pathogenesis:

–inv(14)(q11q32) and t(14;14)(q11;q32) juxtapose TCL1A to the TCR gene enhancer loci of TRA/TRD resulting in constitutive expressions of TCL1 oncogenes leading to dysregulated expression of TCL1 which enhances TCR signaling, inhibit activation-induced death, enhances AKT signaling and increased cell proliferation and survival.

–Mutations and/or deletions of ATM reduces its function  leading to impaired DNA damage repair and cooperates with TCL1 deregulation to accumulate DNA lesions contributing to leukemogenesis.

–Activating mutations of  IL2RG, JAK1/3, and STAT5B genes leads to constitutive STAT5 signaling.

–Mutations in EZH2, FBXW10, and CHEK2  (epigenetic regulation, proteasome degradation, and DNA repair) contribute to the pathogenesis.

–Complex karyotypes, chromosome 8 abnormalities, deletions in 12p13 and 22q, 5p, 6 and 17 abnormalities. 200

Original page 201

•Clinical picture:

–Asymptomatic (30%).

–Hepatosplenomegaly

–Generalized lymphadenopathy.

–Cutaneous involvement

–Malignant effusions

•Laboratory diagnosis: 9

–CBC: Marked lymphocytosis of >100 x 10 /L, anemia and thrombocytopenia due to bone marrow infiltration.

–Serum immunoglobulins are normal

–Morphology:

○Small to medium-sized cells with non-granular basophilic cytoplasm, round, oval or markedly irregular nuclei with visible nucleoli.

○Small cell variant (25%): Relatively small in size with scanty cytoplasm and small nuclei containing condensed chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli

○5% of cases: Neoplastic cells are small to medium-sized with irregular nuclear contours resembling cerebriform cells of Sézary Syndrome and basophilic cytoplasm with protrusions or blebs.

–Bone marrow aspirate: Aggregates of neoplastic lymphoid cells

–Bone marrow core biopsy: Diffuse and interstitial infiltration.

–Immunophenotyping: Mature T-cell immunophenotype of mostly central- memory like differentiation:

○Positive expression of CD2, CD3 (may be weak), CD5, and CD7

○Negative expression of TdT and CD1a.

○CD4+/CD8- (40- 60%), CD4+/CD8+ (25-41%) or CD4-/CD8+ (15%)

○CD52 is usually expressed at a high level

○Overexpression of the oncogene TCL1A. 201

Original page 202

–Genetic tests:

○Clonal TCR gene rearrangements

○Rearrangements involving TCL1 and the TRA/TRD .

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Differential diagnosis:

–Mature T-cell leukemia as ATLL, Sezary Syndrome and T large granular lymphocytic leukemia.

–ALL

–Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma, and mantle cell lymphoma.

•Prognosis:

–Aggressive course (most cases), or stable or slowly progressive (20-30%).

–Adverse prognostic factors include age above 65 years, presence of serous effusions, hepatic or CNS involvement, bulky lymphadenopathy, very high absolute lymphocyte counts, complex karyotype, very high TCL1A protein, bone marrow suppression, or organ dysfunction. 202

Original page 203

•Definition It is a neoplastic proliferation of cytotoxic large granular T cells with 9 persistent peripheral blood absolute (>2x10L) or relative (>50%) lymphocytosis

•Synonym: T-cell lymphoproliferative disease of granular lymphocytes; T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia

•Epidemiology:

–Rare (< 5% of lymphoproliferative disorders) with slightly higher prevalence in Asia.

–It is a disease of adults and rare in individuals <25 years.

–No gender predisposition.

•Etiology: It is frequently associated with autoimmunity, hematolymphoid malignancies, and human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 leads to chronic antigenic stimulation.

•Pathogenesis:

–Chronic antigenic stimulation leads to oligoclonal or clonal expansion of memory effector T-cells and acquired resistance to activation-induced cell death.

–IL-15 and autocrine PDGF stimulation leads to T cell expansion and resistant to Fas-FasL mediated apoptosis.

–Abnormalities in cell-signaling: Constitutive activation of STAT3, with or without mutation increases cellular survival. Abnormalities of PI3K/AKT and NF-kB signaling pathways.

–Other mutations include mutations of T-LGLL are TET2, TNFAIP3, BCL11B, FLT3 and PTPN23 genes. 203

Original page 204

•Clinical picture:

–Asymptomatic (1/3 cases).

–Clinical features of cytopenia: It may be complicated by bleeding complications, transfusion-dependent anemia, aphthous ulcers of oral mucosa and ulceration or recurrent bacterial infections of the skin, oropharynx, or perirectum.

–Fatigue and B-symptoms are not common.

–Autoimmune disorders as Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE and Sjogren syndrome.

–Splenomegaly in some cases.

–Lymphadenopathy and hepatomegaly are rare.

•Laboratory diagnosis: 9

–CBC: Neutropenia (< 1.5x10/L), anemia and thrombocytopenia.

–Abnormal serologic findings indicative of immune activation, such as polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia or positive anti-nuclear antibodies.

–It may be associated with monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis and hematologic malignancies, mostly B-cell lymphomas.

–Morphology: Small, minimally irregular nuclei, condensed chromatin and abundant pale-staining cytoplasm containing variably abundant azurophilic granules.

–Bone marrow examination: Not required but can aid in confirmation of the diagnosis and exclusion of other causes of cytopenias. It is difficult to identify in bone marrow aspirate specimens:

○Slightly hypercellular or may be normocellular or hypocellular.

○Mixed interstitial and intrasinusoidal infiltration of small lymphoid cells without significant atypia. Diffuse infiltration is accompanied by nodular aggregates of small lymphocytes. 204

Original page 205

–Immunophenotyping:

○Most cases are of CD8 positive alpha-beta T-cells with a mature effector memory phenotype (CD3+/CD8+/CD57+/CD45RA+/ CD62L-).  Some cases express CD4 either alone or in association with CD8dim. γ/δ T-cell is present in some cases.

○Positive expression of CD57, CD16, CD2, CD3, CD8, TCRbeta, CD7 and the cytotoxic granule proteins TIA-1, perforin, granzyme B and granzyme M.

○Partial expression of CD8.

○Rare expression of CD56

○Negative expression of CD5.

○The NK-cell associated receptors killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptor (KIR) and CD94/NKG2 are expressed in some cases.

–Genetic tests:

○Monoclonal or oligoclonal TCR gene rearrangement

○STAT3 and STAT5B mutations.

•Diagnostic criteria:

205

Original page 206

•Differential diagnosis:

–Reactive CD8+ T-cell expansions: Autoimmune disorders and chronic infectious states (e.g. HTLV-1): Absence of tissue infiltration other than bone marrow, significant cytopenias, TCR monoclonality and/or STAT3/5B mutation analysis.

–NK-LGLL and mature T-cell neoplasms with leukemic presentation such as T- prolymphocytic leukemia, adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and Sezary syndrome.

•Prognosis:

–Prognosis is good.

–Neutropenia, transfusion-dependent anemia and STAT3 mutation are associated with a worse prognosis.

–Rare cases progress to aggressive T cell lymphoma. 206

Original page 207

•Definition: It is a neoplasm characterized by a persistent increase in peripheral blood 9 NK cells (usually greater than 2x10/L) in the absence of a clearly identifiable cause and a chronic indolent clinical course.

•Synonym: Chronic lymphoproliferative disorder of NK cells and chronic NK-large granular lymphocyte lymphoproliferative disorder

•Epidemiology:

–It is a disease of adults without gender predilection.

–No racial, geographic, or genetic predisposition.

•Etiology: Unknown but may be precipitated by stimulation of innate immunity, possibly by viral infection.

•Pathogenesis:

–Activating mutations of  STAT3

–Mutations in TET2

–Mutations of the gene CCL22 encoding Chemokine (C-C Motif) Ligand 22.

–Mutations in TNFAIP3 and PI-3 kinase pathway genes

–STAT5B mutations are rare.

–Interplay between KIR expressed by the NK-cells and their ability to recognize self-MHC-I. 207

Original page 208

•Clinical picture:

–Most patients are asymptomatic.

–Association with autoimmune disorders, solid tumors, hematologic neoplasms, and neuropathy.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–CBC: Neutropenia and/or anemia.

–Morphology: Intermediate to large cells, with abundant pale-staining cytoplasm and variably abundant azurophilic granules. The granules may be fine to coarse and may be difficult to visualize in some cases. The nuclei are typically small and round with condensed chromatin and minimally irregular nuclear contours.

–Bone marrow aspirate: Lymphocytes may be increased but the cytoplasm is often difficult to visualize.

–Bone marrow biopsy: Intrasinusoidal or interstitial infiltration may also be seen. The infiltrating cells have small, minimally irregular nuclei with lack of distinctive cytologic features.

–Immunophenotyping: 

○CD16 positive and surface CD3 negative with cytoplasmic CD3-epsilon expression may be present.

○CD56 is usually positive, however, approximately 50% of cases show weak or absent expression.

○Diminished expression of CD2 and CD7 and uniform strong expression of CD8.

○Abnormalities in NK-cell receptor expression is a hallmark:

➢Complete lack or restricted killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptor in CD56 negative cases.

➢Uniform, bright CD94/NKG2A heterodimer expression

➢Weak or absent expression of CD161.

○Expression of cytotoxic granule proteins (TIA-1, Granzyme B, Granzyme M). 208

–Genetic tests:

○Mutations of  STAT3 and TET2.

○TCR gene rearrangement: Absence of clonal T-cell populations.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Differential diagnosis:

–Mature T-cell neoplasms with leukemic presentation, in particular T-LGLL: When lymphocytosis is prominent, aggressive NK-cell leukaemia may be considered; NK-LGLL is distinguished by the indolent clinical presentation and lack of nuclear EBV-positivity.

•Prognosis:

–Indolent in 50% of cases

–Cytopenias and recurrent infections have a worse prognosis. 209

•Definition: It is a mature T-cell neoplasm associated with human T-cell leukemia virus type I (HTLV-1).

•Subtypes:

–Smouldering ATLL

–Chronic ATLL: Divided into the unfavorable and favorable subtypes based on the presence of LDH or BUN levels above the normal upper limits or an albumin level below the normal lower limit

–Lymphoma ATLL

–Acute ATLL: Diagnosed by exclusion of the other 3 subtypes.

N.B.: Acute, lymphoma, and unfavourable chronic subtypes of ATLL, which have a similar prognosis, are grouped as aggressive ATLL, while favorable chronic and smouldering ATLLs are grouped as indolent ATLL. 210

Original page 211

•Epidemiology:

–It is endemic (linked to HTLV-1) in several regions of the world, in particular southwestern Japan, the Caribbean, inter-tropical Africa, the Middle East, South America and Papua New Guinea.

–The median age of onset varies by geographic location.

•Etiology: Only 3-5% of HTLV-1 infections develops ATLL:

–Risk factors include male sex, older age, higher HTLV-1 proviral load, longer duration of infection and younger age at acquisition.

–Full transformation requires additional genetic and/or epigenetic events.

•Pathogenesis:

–The Tax protein of HTLV-1 is a transcriptional transactivator, which can activate cellular pathways involved in T-cell proliferation, mainly via the NF-kappa B and AP-1 pathways.

–The HBZ (HTLV-1 B-zip protein) of HTLV-1 drives cell proliferation, inhibits apoptosis and induces TIGIT and CCR4 expression on cell surface, implicated in the proliferation and trafficking of malignant cells.

–Alteration of host genes involved in antigen presentation leads to escape of the cytotoxic T-lymphocytes (CTL).

–Frequent gain-of-function alterations in TCR/NF-kappa B signaling, including activating mutations in PLCG1, PRKCB, and CARD11, and CTLA4::CD28 and ICOS::CD28 fusions, and REL C-terminal truncational changes.

–Immune evasion–related molecules, such as HLA-A and HLA-B, are recurrently altered.

–Other genetic targets include transcription factors (including alterations in CIC- ATXN1 complex and IKZF2 intragenic deletions), transcriptional coregulators (TBL1XR1 alterations), chemokine receptors (CCR4 and CCR7 C-terminal 211

Original page 212

truncating mutations), epigenetic regulators (ARID2 and EP300 alterations), and tumor suppressors (TP53 and CDKN2A alterations).

–Repressive epigenetic changes, such as H3K27 trimethylation and CpG island DNA hypermethylation, which modulate multiple pathways, including NF-kappa B signaling, MHC class I molecules, and Cys2-His2 zinc finger genes involved in retroelement silencing.

•Clinical picture:

–Generalized lymphadenopathy

–Cutaneous lesions

–Hepatosplenomegaly

–Organ infiltration, particularly CNS, gastrointestinal tract, bone, and lung.

–Immunodeficiency, with frequent opportunistic infections caused by Pneumocystis jiroveci, Candida spp., Cytomegalovirus or Strongyloides stercoralis.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–CBC and blood film: Leukocytosis with increased abnormal lymphocytes showing cerebriform or flower-like nuclei and neutrophilia/eosinophilia

–Serum LDH: Elevated

–Soluble interleukin-2 receptor: Elevated

–Hypercalcemia.

–Seropositivity of HTLV1.

–Morphology: Neoplastic lymphoid cells are agranular, medium-sized to large lymphoid cells, with irregular nuclei and basophilic cytoplasm, so called ‘flower cells’ in the acute variant. The cells in the smouldering or chronic variant are generally small, with normal or less atypical appearance. 212

Original page 213

–Immunophenotyping:

○Positive express some pan-T-cell antigens (CD2, CD3, CD5), but usually lack CD7. Most cases are CD4-positive and CD8-negative, but some are CD4- CD8+, double-positive, or double-negative.

○CD25 is expressed in most cases.

○CD30 may be variably positive especially in larger cells, but they are negative for ALK and cytotoxic molecules.

○Tumor cells frequently express CCR4, and a proportion of cells express FOXP3.

○Downregulation of CD7 and upregulation of CCR7 and CADM1 are more frequently observed in aggressive ATLL compared to indolent ATLL.

–Genetic tests: Monoclonal integration of HTLV-1 from the neoplastic T-cells in peripheral blood, and tissue specimens.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Differential diagnosis:

–T-cell lymphoma or leukemia: Sezary syndrome and T-prolymphocytic leukemia: Diagnosis of ATLL is confirmed by the detection of HTLV-1 antibody, or by demonstration of monoclonal integration of pro-viral HTLV-1 DNA.

–Classic Hodgkin lymphoma: Atypia in the lymphoid cells surrounding Hodgkin- Reed-Sternberg (HRS)-like cells could be a clue to identify Hodgkin-like ATLL.

–Anaplastic variant of ATLL should be differentiated from cytotoxic molecule- negative ALK-negative ALCL.

•Prognosis: It depends on disease stage and clinical subtype. 213

•Definition: It is a neoplasm of T lymphocytes defined by the triad of erythroderma; generalized lymphadenopathy; and the presence of clonally related neoplastic T cells with cerebriform nuclei (Sézary cells) in skin, lymph nodes, and peripheral blood.

•Epidemiology:

–It is rare.

–It occurs in adults, characteristically > 60 years.

–It shows a male predominance.

•Etiology: Environmental UV exposure is a key causal factor.

•Pathogenesis:

–The normal counterpart is circulating central memory T cells (CD27+ CD45RA− CD45RO+) or skin-homing CD4+ T cells expressing CLA, CCR4 and CCR7.

–Immunosuppression due to the production of type-2 cytokines (Th2) which suppress Th1 immunity.

–Recurrent gain of function mutations (PLCG1; CARD11; CD28; RLTPR) affect TCR signaling pathways and up-regulate NFkB activity.

–Isochromosome 17q

–Mutations in DNA damage response pathways (TP53; POT1; ATM), JAK-STAT signalling (STAT5B; JAK3) and chromatin modifiers (ARID1A; TRRAP; DNMT3A; TET2).

•Clinical picture:

–Erythroderma, pruritus, alopecia, ectropion, palmar or plantar hyperkeratosis, lichenification and onychodystrophy. Plaques (early stages) and generalized pruritus without erythroderma are rare.

–Generalized lymphadenopathy.

–Increased prevalence of secondary cutaneous and systemic malignancies. 214

Original page 215

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Peripheral blood: Characteristic Sézary cells which are large atypical lymphocytes with irregular contours and deep clefts and abnormally shaped deeply grooved nucleus with nuclear convolutions and are described as “cerebriform nuclei”.

–Bone marrow may be involved with sparse infiltration which is mainly interstitial.

–Immunophenotyping:

○The neoplastic T cells typically show CD3+, CD4+, CD8– phenotype with frequent aberrant loss of pan T-cell antigens such as CD2, CD5, CD7 and/or CD26 in the neoplastic cells.

○Positive expression of PD1 (CD279).

○Positive expression of cutaneous lymphocyte antigen (CLA) and the skin- homing receptor CCR4, as well as CCR7.

○Positive expression of TCRα/β, CD25, ICOS and sometimes CXCL13.

○The natural killer cell markers, CD158K/KIR3DL2 and NKp46 may also be expressed.

–Genetic tests: The tumor cells are clonal by TCR gene rearrangement.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Differential diagnosis:

–SS should be distinguished from inflammatory erythrodermic dermatoses and other haematologic malignancies presenting with erythroderma. Additionally, SS should be distinguished from adult Tcell leukaemia/lymphoma. Benign conditions such as drug reactions, psoriasis, chronic eczema, pityriasis rubra 215

Original page 216

pilaris, scabies, dermatomyositis, lupus, pemphigus foliaceus, and erythematous dermatitis should be excluded. Cytology See description above.

•Prognosis:

–It is an aggressive disease

–Prognosis depends on the stage and the degree of peripheral blood involvement, but the prognostic relevance of bone marrow involvement is unknown.

–Most patients die of opportunistic infections. 216

•Definition: It is a systemic malignant proliferation of NK-cells with an acute presentation and highly aggressive clinical course, and frequent association with Epstein-Barr virus.

•Intravascular NK/T-cell lymphoma (IVNKTCL): It is provisionally included under the category of ANKL. It does not present with mass lesions and shows predilection for skin and CNS. It is a highly aggressive neoplasm with a poor prognosis, especially in patients with multi-system involvement. The pathobiology has been linked to the role of EBV in most cases. Somatic mutations in epigenetic regulators (DDX3X, ARID1A, histone genes) have been identified.

•Epidemiology:

–It is a rare form of leukemia that is more prevalent in Asian populations.

–Patients are most commonly young to middle-aged adults

–No sex predilection.

•Etiology:

–Unknown.

–It may evolve from chronic active EBV disease (90% of cases).

–Exceptional cases may evolve from NK-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia

•Pathogenesis

–EBV infection.

–Cytogenetic abnormalities: del(6)(q21q25), i(7)(q10), de11q, del 7p, del 17p and gains in 1q.

–Mutations in genes encoding components of the JAK/STAT and RAS/MAPK pathways, histone modifying molecules (TET2, CREBBP, KMT2D, DDX3X), and immune checkpoint molecules CD274 (PD-L1)/PDCD1LG2 (PD-L2). TP53 is mutated in one-third of cases. 217

Original page 218

•Clinical picture

–Fever and constitutional symptoms

–Hepatosplenomegaly and jaundice, mimicking hepatitis.

–Lymphadenopathy may be present

–Skin and nasal lesions are uncommon.

–Coagulopathy and multiorgan failure.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Peripheral blood:

○Hemophagocytic syndrome.

○The number of circulating leukaemic cells ranges from low to high, and is below 20% in one-third of patients.

–Morphology: Circulating leukemic cells vary in appearance from cells indistinguishable from normal large granular lymphocytes to cells with atypical nuclei including enlargement, irregular foldings, open chromatin or distinct nucleoli. They have ample pale or lightly basophilic cytoplasm containing fine or coarse azurophilic granules.

–Bone marrow smears: Scanty to abundant leukemic cells, with reactive histiocytes in the background showing hemophagocytosis and frequent apoptosis.

–Bone marrow biopsy: Diffuse or patchy destructive infiltration

–Liver function tests: Abnormal

–Serum FAS ligand: High levels.

–Immunophenotyping:

○The leukaemic cells are typically CD2+, surface CD3-, CD3ε+, CD5-, CD7+ CD16+ CD56+, and positive for cytotoxic molecules (granzyme B, perforin, and/or TIA1).

○CD8 and CD11b may be expressed, while CD57 is usually negative.

○There is lack of T-cell receptor (TCR) protein expression.

○The neoplastic cells express FAS ligand 218

Original page 219

–Genetic tests:

○Germline configuration of T-cell receptor genes supports the NK-cell lineage.

○The majority of cases show positive labeling for EBER (EBV) in leukemic cells on in-situ hybridization.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Differential diagnosis:

–Disseminated ENKTL: ANKL differs in the acute fulminant systemic clinical presentation and lack of nasal involvement.

–NK-LGLL and T-cell LGL leukemia (T-LGLL): They are associated with mild or no symptoms at presentation, lack of morphologic atypia in the circulating LGLs, and lack of EBV; TLGLL is furthermore of T rather than NK lineage.

–Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma: Circulating leukemic cells are uncommon, neoplastic cells are of T-lineage often with TCRγδ expression, EBV is negative, and isochromosome 7q is frequently found.

•Prognosis:

–Fulminant clinical course, often complicated by coagulopathy, multiorgan failure and/or hemophagocytic syndrome.

–Short median survival

–Poor response to chemotherapy

–L-asparaginase containing regimens and allogeneic stem cell transplantation may be curative. 219
